descriptors.title: Designed products and environments
descriptors.description: explore how familiar products, services and environments are designed by people
descriptors.knowledge: This is the first Design and Technologies descriptor in the curriculum. Students have no prior DT knowledge assumed. They bring general familiarity with everyday products and environments. They have not yet connected objects or places to the idea that people deliberately designed and made them for a purpose.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore how familiar products, services and environments are designed by people, identifying that design decisions are made for a purpose.
elaborations: identifying how First Nations Australians have long designed and produced domestic items including clothing, tools and shelter, for example the Lamalama Peoples of the eastern Cape York Peninsula weave the reddish coloured fibres from Acacia latifolia alternately with white coloured fibres from Brachychiton diversifolium to produce a striped woven bag

exploring how local delivery services meet different needs of people, for example describing how gift packages can be sent to and from people who live in different locations and how online shopping items arrive at a person's home
exploring how an environment such as a local playground may have shade structures to protect users and be designed to allow access for all
describing how community gardens, public swimming pools and parks are designed to help people stay healthy

asking questions about the design of products from the local store, for example why certain packaging materials might have been selected, and how people design the text and images on the packaging to attract people's attention

nodes.label: Recognising that products and environments are designed by people
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify familiar products and environments and recognise that they were designed and made by people
criteria: Names at least two designed products or environments
States that people designed and made them — does not treat them as naturally occurring
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a populated category of 'designed by people', Node 2's purpose reasoning has no grounded examples to work with — students cannot explore why design decisions were made if they have not yet reliably identified that objects are designed at all.

width.minimum: Identify at least two familiar products or environments (e.g. playground, packaging, school building) and state that people designed and made them
width.typical: Identify multiple familiar products, services and environments across home and school contexts; explain that each was designed by people; recognise that different things are designed for different reasons
wider: Identify how First Nations Australians have long designed and produced domestic items — for example exploring how the Lamalama Peoples weave bags using fibres from two different plants; discuss what the item was designed for and how the design choices reflect purpose
Explore how a local playground has shade structures designed to protect users and allow access for all — identify specific design decisions and explain why they were made

modes.reason: Students at Foundation may not distinguish between natural objects and designed objects, or may not yet connect a familiar thing (the school building, their lunch box) to the idea that a person made deliberate decisions about it. Accumulating examples across product, service and environment categories builds the category of 'designed by people' before purpose reasoning is introduced.

nodes.label: Exploring design decisions and purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore how a product, service or environment is designed for a purpose — identifying at least one design decision and why it was made
criteria: Identifies at least one design decision in a product or environment
Connects that decision to a purpose — explains why it was designed that way

width.minimum: For one familiar product or environment, identify one design decision and explain what purpose it serves
width.typical: Explore design decisions across multiple products, services and environments; explain how design decisions (materials, shape, features) serve the purpose; ask questions about why things were designed the way they were
wider: Ask questions about the design of products from the local store — why was particular packaging chosen? how do the text and images attract people's attention? connect design decisions to purpose
Explore how community gardens, public swimming pools and parks are designed to help people stay healthy — identify specific design decisions and the purposes they serve
Explore how an online or delivery service is designed to meet people's needs — describe how gift packages are sent between locations and how design decisions make this possible

modes.reason: Connecting a design decision to its purpose requires students to reason from feature to intent — 'the shade structure is there because...' rather than just noticing the shade structure exists. Scaffolding this with a question structure (what is it? who uses it? what does this part do? why?) builds the reasoning habit before the Y1-2 descriptor asks students to connect design to community need and sustainability.

descriptors.title: Design and make solutions
descriptors.description: generate, communicate and evaluate design ideas, and use materials, equipment and steps to safely make a solution for a purpose
descriptors.knowledge: This is the first Design and Technologies process descriptor. Students have no prior design process experience assumed. They bring general play and construction experience. They have not yet framed design as purposeful — generating ideas for a specific purpose, communicating those ideas in a design form, making a solution, or evaluating against a purpose.
descriptors.endpoint: Students generate and communicate at least one design idea for a purpose, use materials and equipment safely to make a solution, and evaluate what they made using personal preferences.
elaborations: identifying a purpose for designing and making a solution, for example the sand keeps blowing out of the sandpit, the birds keep flying into the waste bin and taking food scraps or people with disability need to know where they can park at school

exploring ideas by drawing or modelling and choosing the most suitable idea, for example drawing or modelling designs for bee hotels to attract native bees to the school garden and choosing one to make, and changing perspectives from front view to plan view
evaluating what they have made using personal preferences, for example using a smiley face Likert scale
exploring how available materials can be used or re-used in construction play, for example using blocks and rain gutters or cardboard to make a ramp to roll a ball or toy car down

practising a range of technical skills safely using equipment, for example joining techniques when making a product from materials, such as a greenhouse to keep a seedling warm or a trellis for holding up tomato plants
assembling components of systems and checking they function as planned, for example making and testing a bowling, stacking or obstacle game with discarded food containers or packaging

nodes.label: Identifying a purpose and generating ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a purpose for designing and making, and generate at least one idea for a solution
criteria: States a purpose for their design (what it is for or what problem it solves)
Generates at least one idea for a solution to that purpose
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a purpose-grounded design idea, Node 2 (communicating a design idea) and Node 3 (making) have no design intent to express or realise — purposeless communication and making is construction play, not design.

width.minimum: Identify a purpose for a design task (what problem or need is being addressed); generate at least one idea for a solution
width.typical: Identify a purpose for designing and making; generate and explore multiple ideas through drawing, modelling or describing; choose the most suitable idea with a reason
wider: Identify a real purpose from the school environment (e.g. sand blowing out of sandpit, birds getting into waste bins, accessibility needs at school) — generate ideas that directly address the identified purpose
Draw or model designs for bee hotels to attract native bees to the school garden — generate multiple ideas and choose one, changing perspectives from front view to plan view

modes.reason: Foundation students readily generate ideas but often skip connecting them to a purpose — the idea exists without a 'what is it for'. Multiple design contexts where the purpose is clearly defined before generating ideas builds the habit of purpose-grounded design thinking rather than open-ended construction play.

nodes.label: Communicating design ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can communicate a design idea through drawing or modelling
criteria: Produces a drawing or model that represents their design idea
Can explain at least one feature of the drawing or model
nodes.hinge_reason: The communicated design idea is the raw material for Node 3 making — without an externalised representation, making is undirected and cannot be checked against a design intent. Node 3 requires something to make toward.

width.minimum: Represent a design idea through at least one drawing or model
width.typical: Communicate a design idea using drawing or modelling; include basic features or labels; explain the design idea to others
wider: Draw or model a ramp design for rolling a ball or toy car — show key features and explain how the design serves the purpose
Model a design for a greenhouse or trellis using available materials — describe what each part is for

modes.reason: Design communication at Foundation requires students to externalise a mental idea into a physical representation. This is a challenging early skill — the gap between what students imagine and what they can draw or model is significant. Repeated practice across different design contexts builds fluency in using drawing/modelling as a thinking and communication tool.

nodes.label: Making a solution safely
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use materials, equipment and steps to safely make a designed solution
criteria: Uses at least one material and one tool or piece of equipment
Follows safety expectations for the tools and materials used

width.minimum: Use at least one material and one piece of equipment to make a solution; follow safety expectations for the tools or equipment used
width.typical: Use materials, components and equipment to make a solution across multiple construction contexts (joining, assembling, constructing); follow safety expectations; check that the solution functions as planned
wider: Use available or re-used materials in construction play — for example blocks, rain gutters or cardboard to make a ramp; explore how different materials affect how the solution works
Make and test a bowling, stacking or obstacle game with discarded food containers — assemble components and check they function as planned

modes.reason: Safe use of materials and equipment is a procedural and behavioural skill requiring consistent practice. Joining techniques, safe cutting, careful assembly — these need repetition across different making contexts before students can execute safely without active teacher supervision. Consolidation is the primary response; width adds variety of materials and contexts.

nodes.label: Evaluating the solution
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate what they made using personal preferences
criteria: Shares at least one opinion about their design or solution
Opinion is connected to the design — not just 'I like it' in general

width.minimum: Share at least one opinion about their design or solution — what they like, what worked or what they would change
width.typical: Evaluate the solution using personal preferences — describe what works well and what could be improved; use a simple evaluation tool (e.g. smiley face Likert scale) to record a judgement; connect evaluation to the original purpose
wider: Record evaluation using audio-recording or video-recording software — describe design strengths and weaknesses and what they would change
Explain how the equipment in a playground might be unsuitable for some children and suggest areas for design improvement — connecting personal evaluation to broader user needs

modes.reason: Evaluation at Foundation requires students to step back from making and judge their output against something — a preference, a purpose, a criterion. Without scaffolding, students tend to say 'I like it' without connecting to purpose or identifying anything to improve. A question structure (what did you want it to do? did it? what would you change?) builds evaluative reasoning rather than just approval.

descriptors.title: Designed solutions for needs
descriptors.description: identify how familiar products, services and environments are designed and produced by people to meet personal or local community needs and sustainability
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore how familiar products, services and environments are designed by people (AC9TDEFK01). They can identify design decisions and connect them to a purpose. They have not yet connected design to community-level needs or to sustainability considerations.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify how familiar products, services and environments are designed and produced to meet personal or local community needs, including sustainability.
elaborations: exploring how First Nations Australians have long understood their dependence on living systems to meet their local and community needs, for example exploring the material culture of the Ngarrindjeri Peoples who sustainably make woven items from a grass-like sedge

exploring how particular services meet different needs of people in the community, for example describing why doctors provide medical care to people in many ways including by phone, video conference, plane, car or outdoor clinic

asking questions about the design of a range of shelters provided for the public and how they meet the needs of people in the community, for example the structures of a school or local sportsground or how to improve accessibility

exploring how local products are designed, for example brainstorming the materials and processes needed to create a costume for a school or community event including using recycled clothing or components to minimise waste
exploring how people come up with new ideas or modify existing designs, for example preventing water wastage when caring for plants

nodes.label: Identifying community needs that design addresses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a personal or local community need and explain how a familiar product, service or environment is designed to meet it
criteria: Names a specific community need (not just a use)
Explains how a product, service or environment is designed to meet that need

width.minimum: Identify one community need (e.g. medical care, shelter, healthy food access) and explain how a product, service or environment is designed to meet it
width.typical: Identify community needs across multiple contexts (health, shelter, food, communication, community access); explain how specific design and production decisions address each need; compare how the same need is met in different ways
wider: Explore how First Nations Australians have long understood their dependence on living systems — for example how the Ngarrindjeri Peoples sustainably make woven items from a grass-like sedge; identify the community need being met and how the design reflects that need
Ask questions about the design of shelters in public spaces (school, sportsground) — identify the community need and how the shelter design addresses it including accessibility

modes.reason: Students readily identify that products exist for a purpose but often describe use rather than need — 'it's for sleeping' rather than 'it meets the community's need for shelter'. Multiple community contexts (medical care, shelter, food production, communication) where the need is explicitly named before the design is examined builds the need-first reasoning habit.

nodes.label: Understanding sustainability in design
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify sustainability considerations in how products are designed and produced
criteria: Identifies at least one sustainability consideration in a design context
Explains why that consideration matters — what environmental impact it addresses

width.minimum: Identify at least one example of sustainability in a design or production context — for example using recycled materials, minimising waste, or protecting a living system
width.typical: Identify sustainability considerations across multiple design contexts; explain why sustainability matters in design and production; give examples of design decisions that minimise negative environmental impact
wider: Explore how people come up with new ideas or modify existing designs to prevent water wastage — identify the sustainability problem, the design response and why it matters

Explore how local products are designed with waste minimisation in mind — for example using recycled clothing or components when making a costume for a community event; explain the sustainability benefit

modes.reason: Sustainability is an abstract concept at Y1-2 level. Students need multiple concrete examples where a specific environmental impact is visible before they can generalise the idea. Water wastage, recycled materials and protected living systems are distinct entry points — each makes a different aspect of sustainability tangible.

descriptors.title: Materials affect movement
descriptors.description: explore how technologies including materials affect movement in products
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore how products are designed by people (AC9TDEFK01). They have made simple solutions using materials (AC9TDEFP01). They have not yet systematically connected material properties to movement outcomes, or explored how changing materials or forces changes how a product moves.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore how material properties and forces affect movement in products, and explain how changing materials can change how a product moves.
elaborations: investigating First Nations Australians' instructive toys and how such toys are designed and made to produce movement, for example propeller toys made from pandanus across northern Australia
selecting materials to show how material properties are appropriate for particular designed solutions, for example materials that enable sliding, floating or flying
exploring how to manipulate materials using a range of tools, equipment and techniques to create movement, for example when constructing a toy boat that floats or a kite that flies
exploring a system such as a marionette or Indonesian wayang kulit shadow puppet to see that by combining materials with forces movement can be created
testing materials to see how they affect movement and speed, for example the movement of a wheeled toy on different surfaces such as timber, carpet, rubber and plastic

nodes.label: Material properties and movement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how a material's properties affect how a product moves
criteria: Names at least one material property
Explains how that property affects how a product moves
nodes.hinge_reason: Without the material-property concept, Node 2's integration of material properties with forces has no anchor — students who cannot generalise from specific examples to a property cannot reason about how property and force interact.

width.minimum: Identify at least one material property (e.g. smooth, rough, flexible, rigid) and explain how it affects movement in a product or on a surface
width.typical: Explore multiple material properties (smooth/rough, light/heavy, flexible/rigid) and explain how each affects movement; select materials to show how properties are appropriate for particular movement outcomes (sliding, floating, flying)
wider: Investigate First Nations Australians' instructive toys and how they are designed and made to produce movement — for example propeller toys made from pandanus across northern Australia; identify which materials are used and how their properties create the movement
Test a wheeled toy on different surfaces (timber, carpet, rubber, plastic) — measure or observe differences in movement and speed; explain how surface material properties affect movement

modes.reason: Students at Y1-2 may connect a specific material to a specific toy without generalising to the property relationship — 'the smooth floor makes it go fast' without understanding that smoothness (low friction) is the relevant property. Multiple material-movement contexts where the same property appears in different products builds the generalised property concept.

nodes.label: Combining materials and forces to create movement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore how combining materials with forces creates movement in a product
criteria: Identifies both a material and a force involved in a product's movement
Explains how the material and force combine to produce the movement

width.minimum: Using one product (e.g. a toy boat, kite or puppet), identify the materials used and explain how force and material combine to create movement
width.typical: Manipulate materials using tools and techniques to create different types of movement across multiple products; explore how combining materials with forces (push, pull, gravity, wind) creates and controls movement; explain the relationship between materials, forces and movement
wider: Explore a marionette or Indonesian wayang kulit shadow puppet — identify how combining materials with forces creates movement; explain how the design enables the operator to control the movement
Construct a toy boat that floats or a kite that flies — select materials deliberately for their movement-enabling properties and explain the material and force choices

modes.reason: At this node, material properties (node 1) and forces must be coordinated simultaneously to understand movement in a product. Neither alone explains movement — it is the interaction of material properties with applied forces that produces the outcome. Integration failure looks like: identifying the material or the force separately without explaining how they combine.

descriptors.title: Growing plants and animals
descriptors.description: explore how plants and animals are grown for food, clothing and shelter
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored how products are designed and produced to meet community needs (AC9TDE2K01). They understand that design decisions connect to purpose. They have not yet examined the origins of the materials used in products — specifically that plants and animals are deliberately grown and managed as sources for food, clothing and shelter.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore how plants and animals are grown and used as sources for food, clothing and shelter, identifying specific plants and animals and the products derived from them.
elaborations: exploring how First Nations Australians grow plants and animals for food, for example how land is transformed through the construction of terraces at Wagadagam on Mabuiag Island in the Torres Strait, or how the Kombumerri Peoples of South East Queensland developed an important aquaculture industry farming mangrove worms
identifying which plants and animals can provide food or materials for clothing and shelter, for example looking at a range of items and sorting them according to plant or animal source

exploring where plants and animals are grown for food, clothing and shelter in Australia, for example citrus fruit in South Australia; cotton in New South Wales, which is harvested and made into yarn and fabric for clothing; or timber for building homes from sustainable forests in Tasmania
identifying products that can be designed and produced from plants and animals, for example food products, paper and wood products, fabrics and yarns

considering a range of tools and equipment that can be used to grow plants for a purpose and their suitability, for example naming and describing tools such as a spade or rake used to cultivate or mulch a home vegetable garden, or equipment such as a seed spreader or global positioning system (GPS) tractor to sow wheat, or a tubestock planting tool and drones to manage forestry plantations

nodes.label: Plants and animals as sources for products
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify which plants and animals provide food, materials for clothing, or materials for shelter
criteria: Names at least one plant and one animal used as a source for food, clothing or shelter
Identifies at least one product derived from each source
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a populated repertoire of plant and animal sources, Node 2 (how and where they are grown) has no examples to explore — students cannot investigate growing methods for sources they have not yet identified.

width.minimum: Sort at least three familiar items into plant-source or animal-source categories; name one plant and one animal used as a source for food, clothing or shelter
width.typical: Identify a range of plants and animals as sources across food, clothing and shelter categories; give examples of products derived from each source; explain the relationship between the plant or animal and the product
wider: Explore how First Nations Australians grow plants and animals for food — for example the aquaculture industry of the Kombumerri Peoples farming mangrove worms, or land transformation through terraces at Wagadagam; identify specific plants or animals and the products they provide
Identify products that can be designed and produced from plants and animals — food products, paper and wood products, fabrics and yarns; trace one product from source to finished item

modes.reason: Students need a range of plant-source and animal-source examples before they can generalise the concept that living things are grown and managed for production purposes. A single example (cows for milk) does not build the category. Accumulating examples across food, clothing and shelter contexts builds the breadth needed for the 'explore' command term.

nodes.label: How and where plants and animals are grown
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore how and where plants and animals are grown for food, clothing and shelter in Australia
criteria: Names at least one location in Australia where a plant or animal is grown
Describes how it is grown or managed for its purpose

width.minimum: Identify where at least one plant or animal is grown in Australia and describe how it is grown or managed for a purpose
width.typical: Explore how plants and animals are grown in different Australian regions for different purposes — citrus in South Australia, cotton in NSW, timber in Tasmania; describe how tools and equipment are used in growing and harvesting; connect growing methods to the product produced
wider: Compare traditional and contemporary growing methods for the same product — for example hand tools versus GPS-guided tractors for wheat; identify how technology changes what is possible
Consider a range of tools used to grow plants for a purpose — from home garden tools (spade, rake) to large-scale equipment (seed spreader, drone); explain what each tool enables and why it is used

modes.reason: Students often have a home-garden mental model for how plants are grown — small, familiar, manual. Encountering growing at different scales (home garden vs cotton farm vs forestry plantation) in different Australian regions builds a more accurate and varied understanding of food and materials production.

descriptors.title: Selecting and preparing food
descriptors.description: explore how food can be selected and prepared for healthy eating
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored how plants and animals are grown for food (AC9TDE2K03). They can identify plant and animal food sources. They have not yet organised foods into health categories or connected preparation methods to healthy eating outcomes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore how foods can be selected and prepared for healthy eating, identifying food groups and preparation methods.
elaborations: identifying a wide range of foods, categorising them into food groups according to the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating and discussing ways to eat a variety of food groups, including cooking methods, tools and equipment needed to prepare them for healthy eating

exploring how people including peoples from the countries of Asia design and produce food for healthy eating based on the available plants and animals in their region, the influence of cultural practices, and locally available tools and equipment

exploring the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Guide to Healthy Eating and identifying foods in each of the 5 food groups which contribute to health and wellbeing, for example choosing foods from each of the 5 food groups which they are familiar with and designing a menu for a day

exploring the local supermarket to observe the variety of foods and the placement of foods on shelves, in aisles and displays; and considering how their design may influence the purchase of foods for healthy food eating

exploring different ways of preparing the products from the school kitchen garden, farmers' market or supermarket, for example preparing vegetables for a salad, steaming or roasting vegetables and noticing the changes in flavour and texture

nodes.label: Selecting foods for healthy eating
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a range of foods and categorise them into food groups for healthy eating
criteria: Correctly categorises at least three foods into food groups
Names at least two different food groups

width.minimum: Identify at least three familiar foods and categorise them into food groups using the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating
width.typical: Identify a wide range of foods and categorise them into the 5 food groups; discuss ways to eat a variety of food groups; begin to design a simple menu that includes multiple food groups
wider: Explore both the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Guide to Healthy Eating — identify foods in each of the 5 food groups from both guides; compare foods that are familiar to different communities
Explore how people from countries of Asia select food for healthy eating based on available plants and animals and cultural practices — identify similarities and differences with the Australian guide
Explore the local supermarket to observe the variety and placement of foods — consider how shelf design may influence food selection for healthy eating

modes.reason: Students readily categorise foods they personally eat but struggle with the full range of food groups when their exposure is narrow. Multiple food contexts — including foods from First Nations and Asian food traditions — builds a richer, less culturally narrow understanding of 'healthy eating'.

nodes.label: Preparing food for healthy eating
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore different ways food can be prepared and connect preparation methods to healthy eating
criteria: Names at least two preparation methods
Explains how at least one preparation method changes the food

width.minimum: Identify at least two ways food can be prepared (e.g. raw, steamed, roasted, sliced); explain how preparation changes the food
width.typical: Explore different preparation methods (raw, steaming, roasting, slicing, cooking) and how each changes the food's flavour, texture or nutritional value; prepare a simple food product using appropriate tools and equipment; connect preparation choices to healthy eating
wider: Prepare vegetables in different ways (e.g. raw salad versus roasted) — compare the changes in flavour and texture and discuss how preparation affects how we experience food
Prepare a food product from a school kitchen garden, farmers' market or supermarket — identify the preparation steps, tools needed and connect to healthy eating

modes.reason: Food preparation involves procedural skills — safe handling, correct use of tools, following steps in order. These require practice across multiple preparation tasks to build the consistent safety habits and procedural fluency needed. Consolidation is the primary response; width adds preparation contexts.

descriptors.title: Describe, draw and model ideas
descriptors.description: generate and communicate design ideas through describing, drawing or modelling, including using digital tools
descriptors.knowledge: Students can generate and communicate design ideas through drawing or modelling (AC9TDEFP01). They have communicated ideas for a purpose. They have not yet labelled drawings, shown multiple views, used digital tools to communicate design ideas, or compared existing products to generate new ideas.
descriptors.endpoint: Students generate and communicate design ideas through describing, drawing or modelling — including labelled drawings with multiple views and using digital tools.
elaborations: comparing and contrasting features of existing products to develop new ideas, for example designing and making a puppet with a movable part after experimenting with other toys with several movable parts

communicating design ideas by modelling or producing and labelling 2-dimensional drawings using a range of technologies, for example designing a new environment such as a cubbyhouse or animal shelter and showing different views (top view and side view) with descriptions of materials and features
communicating an opinion about their design ideas, for example expressing own likes and dislikes about a design idea for felt finger puppets including how they have made changes to their design ideas
describing the results from exploring design ideas, for example recording the results from people taste-testing a food product

nodes.label: Generating ideas from existing products
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare and contrast features of existing products to generate new design ideas
criteria: Identifies at least one feature of an existing product
Generates a design idea that connects to or builds on what was observed
nodes.hinge_reason: Without analytical observation of existing products to generate design ideas, Node 2's labelled drawings have no design rationale — students who copy rather than adapt cannot produce drawings that explain design decisions.

width.minimum: Examine at least one existing product and identify at least one feature that could inform a new design idea
width.typical: Compare and contrast features of multiple existing products to develop new ideas; identify what works well and what could be different; use observations to generate at least one design idea that builds on or modifies what they have seen
wider: Compare features of several toys with movable parts — identify what makes the movement work; use this to design a new product (e.g. a puppet) with a movable part inspired by observations
Record the results from exploring design ideas (e.g. from people taste-testing a food product) — use the results to inform a revised design idea

modes.reason: Generating ideas from existing products requires students to reason analytically before generating — identifying which features matter and why. Without this scaffold, students copy rather than adapt, or generate ideas unconnected to what they observed. A sequence (observe → identify what works → identify what could change → generate new idea) builds design thinking rather than copying.

nodes.label: Communicating design ideas through labelled drawings and modelling
nodes.checkpoint: Students can communicate a design idea through a labelled 2D drawing or model, including showing different views and describing materials and features
criteria: Produces a drawing or model that others can interpret
Includes at least one label or description of a feature or material
nodes.hinge_reason: Labelled drawings are the communication vehicle for Node 3's digital tool integration — without fluency in producing interpretable labelled drawings, there is no design idea for students to communicate using digital tools.

width.minimum: Produce a drawing or model of a design idea that includes at least one label or description of a feature
width.typical: Produce labelled 2D drawings of design ideas using different views (top and side); describe materials and features; produce a model or drawing that someone else could understand; include dimensions or scale where appropriate
wider: Design a new environment (e.g. cubbyhouse or animal shelter) — show different views (top and side) with descriptions of materials and features for each view
Design felt finger puppets — communicate design ideas with labels showing how movable parts work; include notes about changes made to the original idea and why

modes.reason: Drawing with labels and showing multiple views requires spatial reasoning and drawing skills that develop through repeated practice. Students need to practise producing labelled drawings across different design contexts before the combination of views, labels and descriptions becomes fluent.

nodes.label: Using digital tools to communicate design ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a digital tool to communicate or record a design idea
criteria: Uses at least one digital tool to communicate a design idea
The digital output represents a design decision or idea, not just a picture of the product

width.minimum: Use at least one digital tool to communicate or represent a design idea (e.g. take a photo, use drawing software, record an opinion about a design)
width.typical: Use digital tools alongside drawn and modelled communications — photograph work in progress, use drawing apps, record audio or video opinions about design ideas; integrate digital communication into the design process
wider: Express opinions about a design idea for felt finger puppets using audio or video — describe what they like and dislike and what changes they have made; play back and reflect
Use digital tools to record results from design experiments (e.g. taste testing) and use the recorded results to communicate a revised design decision

modes.reason: Digital tools are a communication medium for design ideas — not a separate activity. At this node, students must integrate digital communication with the design ideas developed in nodes 1 and 2. Integration failure looks like: using digital tools in isolation from the design process, or treating photography as separate from communicating design thinking.

descriptors.title: Safely make designed solutions
descriptors.description: use materials, components, tools, equipment and techniques to safely make designed solutions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use materials and equipment to make solutions safely (AC9TDEFP01). They have practised basic joining and construction techniques. They have not yet deliberately selected materials for a purpose, or demonstrated safe use of a range of tools and techniques across different construction contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use materials, components, tools, equipment and techniques to safely make designed solutions across different construction contexts.
elaborations: exploring how available materials can be used or re-used in construction play, for example using used wrapping paper and gift cards to design and make decorations or signage for the classroom or a school event to minimise waste
practising a range of technical skills using tools and equipment safely, for example joining techniques when making products, watering and mulching gardens, preparing a recipe using a knife safely
assembling components and checking they function as planned, for example containers, contents and joining materials when making musical shakers

nodes.label: Selecting and using materials for a purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify appropriate materials for a designed solution and explain why they are suitable
criteria: Names at least one material selected for the task
Gives at least one reason why that material is appropriate for the purpose
nodes.hinge_reason: Material selection reasoning feeds directly into Node 2's safe making — students who select materials by preference rather than suitability are likely to attempt construction with inappropriate materials, creating safety risks and non-functional outcomes.

width.minimum: Select at least one material for a construction task and state one reason why it is appropriate for the purpose
width.typical: Select materials, components and joining materials appropriate for the design; explain why each material suits the purpose; consider re-use of available materials where appropriate
wider: Explore how available materials can be re-used — for example using wrapping paper and gift cards to make classroom decorations; explain how re-use minimises waste
Select materials to show how properties are appropriate for particular designed solutions — materials that enable sliding, floating or flying

modes.reason: Material selection requires students to reason from purpose to property — 'I need it to float, so I need a material that is light and waterproof'. Without this scaffold, students select materials by preference or availability rather than suitability. A reasoning sequence (what does it need to do? what material property is needed? which materials have that property?) builds deliberate selection.

nodes.label: Using tools and techniques safely
nodes.checkpoint: Students can practise a range of technical skills using tools and equipment safely
criteria: Uses at least two tools or techniques correctly and safely
Follows safety expectations for each tool — no unsafe actions observed

width.minimum: Use at least two tools or techniques safely in a construction context (e.g. cutting, joining, measuring, planting, preparing food with a knife)
width.typical: Practise a range of technical skills across different construction contexts — joining techniques, watering and mulching gardens, preparing a recipe using a knife safely; follow safety expectations consistently
wider: Assemble components for a musical shaker (container, contents, joining materials) — check they function as planned after assembly; explain the joining technique used and why it was chosen
Use joining techniques when making a product from multiple materials — identify which joining technique is appropriate for each material pair and explain why

modes.reason: Safe tool use is a procedural skill requiring consistent, repeated practice across different tools and materials. Each tool or technique has its own safety requirements and physical demands. Consolidation here is the primary response — accuracy, consistency and safety develop through practice, not through encountering more contexts.

descriptors.title: Evaluate success and sustainability
descriptors.description: evaluate the success of design ideas and solutions based on personal preferences and including sustainability
descriptors.knowledge: Students can evaluate what they made using personal preferences (AC9TDEFP01). They have shared opinions about their design. They have not yet evaluated against sustainability considerations, reflected on environmental impacts, or compared design ideas for strengths and weaknesses in a structured way.
descriptors.endpoint: Students evaluate the success of design ideas and solutions based on personal preferences and sustainability considerations.
elaborations: reflecting on and recording a judgement about design ideas, for example describing how design ideas meet the needs of those who will use the solution using audio-recording or video-recording software
sharing design strengths and weaknesses, for example explaining how the equipment in a playground might be unsuitable for some children to use and suggesting areas for design improvement

reflecting on the environmental impacts of the production of a solution and considering alternative approaches that would minimise future negative impacts, for example identifying the negative environmental impacts of different food packaging and how these could be minimised

reflecting on the challenges of designing and producing a solution and recording these reflections, for example when growing a food product, designing a structure to take a load or making a nutritious snack

nodes.label: Evaluating against personal preferences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on and record a judgement about a design idea or solution based on personal preferences, identifying strengths and areas for improvement
criteria: Names at least one strength of the design or solution
Names at least one area for improvement — not just 'make it better' but a specific change
nodes.hinge_reason: Evaluative reasoning against personal preferences is the prerequisite for Node 2's sustainability evaluation — Node 2 extends the same reasoning structure to environmental criteria. Students who cannot evaluate against any criterion cannot take on a second, less familiar one.

width.minimum: Describe at least one strength and one weakness of a design or solution using personal preferences as the basis
width.typical: Reflect on design ideas and solutions across the full design process — describe what meets the design need and what could be improved; record judgements using audio, video or written/drawn responses; share with others
wider: Describe how design ideas meet the needs of those who will use the solution — use audio or video recording to capture the evaluation; review the recording and identify changes
Share design strengths and weaknesses with the class — explain how playground equipment might be unsuitable for some children and suggest specific improvements

modes.reason: Evaluation requires students to apply a criterion to their work — but at Y1-2, the criterion of personal preference is itself vague without scaffolding. A structure (what did you want it to do? does it do that? what would you change and why?) moves evaluation from 'I like it/I don't like it' to reasoned judgement about design success.

nodes.label: Evaluating sustainability impacts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on the environmental impacts of a solution and consider alternative approaches that minimise negative impacts
criteria: Identifies at least one environmental impact of a production activity
Suggests at least one concrete alternative that would reduce that impact

width.minimum: Identify at least one environmental impact of making a solution and suggest one way that impact could be reduced
width.typical: Reflect on environmental impacts across multiple production contexts (food packaging, material waste, water use); identify negative impacts and suggest alternative approaches; connect sustainability evaluation to both design ideas and making processes
wider: Identify the negative environmental impacts of different food packaging options — suggest how packaging could be redesigned to minimise impact; explain the trade-offs
Reflect on the challenges of producing a solution (growing food, making a structure, preparing a snack) and record what would be done differently to reduce environmental impact next time

modes.reason: Sustainability impacts are not immediately visible at Y1-2 level — students need to encounter them in multiple, concrete production contexts before the evaluative habit generalises. Food packaging, water use and material waste are distinct enough to reveal different aspects of environmental impact, each making the abstract concept tangible.

descriptors.title: Sequence making steps cooperatively
descriptors.description: sequence steps for making designed solutions cooperatively
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use materials and equipment to make solutions (AC9TDEFP01, AC9TDE2P02). They have followed steps to make things. They have not yet formally sequenced steps for making as a planning activity, recorded procedures, or identified roles for cooperative group making.
descriptors.endpoint: Students sequence the steps for making a designed solution and work cooperatively with others, identifying roles within a group.
elaborations: using lists or storyboarding when planning and making, for example when creating an electronic planting calendar
recording the procedure for making a product, for example the ordered steps for making a salad, instructions for making a container or bag
identifying roles for each member of a group when working cooperatively, for example when making a number of items for a school fete

nodes.label: Sequencing making steps
nodes.checkpoint: Students can sequence the steps needed to make a designed solution in a logical order
criteria: Sequences at least four steps in a logical order
Can explain why at least one step must come before another
nodes.hinge_reason: Step sequencing is the planning input for Node 2's cooperative role assignment — without a sequence to distribute across group members, roles cannot be meaningfully identified and the cooperative making has no structure.

width.minimum: Sequence at least four steps for making a simple product in the correct order; explain why the order matters
width.typical: Use lists or storyboarding to plan and sequence steps for making across different production contexts; record the procedure; explain why steps must be in a particular order and what happens if they are not
wider: Record the ordered steps for making a salad or other food preparation task — describe each step and explain what would happen if the order changed
Create a planning list or storyboard for an electronic planting calendar — sequence the steps and explain the order decisions

modes.reason: Step sequencing in design feels obvious for simple tasks but students often conflate steps with materials or confuse what to do with when to do it. Multiple production contexts — food preparation (where order is safety-critical), construction (where joins must be made before assembly), garden tasks — each expose different dimensions of why sequence matters.

nodes.label: Working cooperatively with identified roles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify roles for group members and work cooperatively toward a shared making outcome
criteria: Carries out an identified role in a cooperative making task
The group's shared output is produced — the cooperative process functioned

width.minimum: Participate in a cooperative making task where roles are identified; carry out at least one assigned role
width.typical: Identify roles for each group member appropriate to the task; work cooperatively toward a shared goal; adjust roles or steps as needed when problems arise
wider: Make a number of items for a school event with a group — assign roles (cutting, joining, decorating, checking), carry out the assigned role and explain how each role contributes to the shared outcome
Write instructions for making a container or bag — include who does each step (role) and in what order; test whether another group can follow the instructions

modes.reason: Cooperative making requires students to coordinate sequenced steps (node 1) with distributed roles — two understandings that must work together. Integration failure looks like: students who can sequence steps individually but cannot coordinate with others (duplicating work, waiting, doing steps in the wrong order because communication broke down).

descriptors.title: Design occupations and sustainability
descriptors.description: examine design and technologies occupations and factors including sustainability that impact on the design of products, services and environments to meet community needs
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify how familiar products, services and environments are designed and produced by people to meet personal or local community needs and sustainability (AC9TDE2K01). They have not yet examined occupations in design and technologies or analysed how sustainability factors actively shape design decisions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students examine design and technologies occupations and the role sustainability plays in shaping what those occupations produce, explaining how products, services and environments are designed to meet community needs.
elaborations: exploring how many First Nations Australians were and continue to be recognised for their specialist skills in designing and producing products made from local materials and providing related services, using sustainable practices to ensure future access to meet community needs, for example traditional adhesives

exploring how design and technologies occupations in the local area (urban, suburban, regional or rural) meet community needs, for example bakers, builders, engineers, farmers, seafood industry workers, mechanics, radiographers, textile designers and others in science, technology, engineering and mathematics roles

examining the suitability of a service or system and proposing improvements, for example a water-saving system for a bathroom at home or school, traffic management systems to reduce traffic jams around the school, remote and regional services including medical services

exploring how Australian designers consider sustainability when designing products, services or environments, for example designing products from 100% recycled materials, designing services that use minimal energy, or designing landscapes that require minimal water

examining products and environments to discover the factors that may have influenced the design and, choice of technologies used, for example discussing energy-efficient cooking with a wok, or sustainable wood products for home use including furniture made from plantation timbers, bamboo toothbrushes or coconut shell bowls
conducting a survey to identify a community need that involves accessibility and social sustainability, for example design features that improve access to the school

nodes.label: Design and technologies occupations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name and describe a range of design and technologies occupations and explain what community need each addresses
criteria: Names at least two distinct design and technologies occupations
Connects each occupation to a community need it addresses
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot connect occupations to community needs cannot examine in N2 and N3 how factors (including sustainability) shape what occupations produce — the factor analysis requires knowing what the occupation is trying to achieve.

width.minimum: Name at least two design and technologies occupations and describe what community need each one addresses
width.typical: Describe a range of design and technologies occupations across different sectors (bakers, builders, engineers, farmers, textile designers, mechanics, radiographers); explain what each occupation produces and who benefits in the community
wider: Explore how many First Nations Australians have been and continue to be recognised for specialist skills in designing and producing products from local materials — investigate specific examples and discuss how these occupations serve community needs
Survey the design and technologies occupations present in the local area (urban, suburban, regional or rural) — discuss how the mix of occupations reflects local community needs and geography

nodes.label: Sustainability as a design factor
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what sustainability means in a design context and give an example of a design decision that reflects sustainability considerations
criteria: Names at least one sustainability factor (e.g. recycled materials, minimal waste, energy use)
Connects that factor to a specific design decision
nodes.hinge_reason: Students without a working understanding of sustainability as a design factor cannot complete the multi-factor analysis in N3 — sustainability is one of the named factors and must be identified alongside others.

width.minimum: Describe one example of a design decision that was shaped by sustainability (e.g. using recycled materials, minimal water use) and explain why the designer made that choice
width.typical: Explain how Australian designers consider sustainability when designing products, services and environments; describe examples across different design types (products from recycled materials, services using minimal energy, landscapes requiring minimal water)
wider: Examine how First Nations Australians use sustainable practices when designing and producing products from local materials — explore how sustainability is embedded in traditional design knowledge and how this knowledge continues today
Investigate a specific sustainability challenge in the local community (e.g. water saving, traffic management, accessibility) and examine what design factors would need to be considered to address it

modes.reason: Students often reduce sustainability to recycling. Examining sustainability across different design domains — products, services, environments, energy, water, materials — builds a broader and more accurate understanding of what sustainability means as a design consideration.

nodes.label: Factors that influence design outcomes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine a product, service or environment and identify factors (beyond sustainability) that influenced its design
criteria: Identifies at least one design factor beyond sustainability
Explains how that factor influenced a specific design decision

width.minimum: Examine one product or environment and identify at least one factor other than sustainability that influenced how it was designed (e.g. who it is for, available materials, cost, culture)
width.typical: Examine a range of products and environments to discover the factors that shaped their design — including community need, material availability, cultural context, energy efficiency and aesthetic considerations; explain how these factors interact
wider: Examine products from an Asian country alongside Australian products — compare the design factors each reflects (materials, cultural context, production methods) and discuss why similar needs are met with different designs

Examine a system or service proposed for improvement (e.g. a water-saving bathroom system, a school traffic management system) — analyse what factors constrain the design and what factors offer opportunity for change

modes.reason: Students at this level can identify features of a product but need scaffolding to move from observation ('it has wheels') to design factor analysis ('wheels were chosen because the product needs to move over different surfaces'). Structured examination routines help students develop analytical habits.

This node integrates occupational knowledge (node 1) with sustainability knowledge (node 2) into a complete factor analysis — students are now examining how multiple factors interact to shape a design outcome. The coordination across factors is the learning.

descriptors.title: Forces and material properties
descriptors.description: describe how forces and the properties of materials affect function in a product or system
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore how technologies including materials affect movement in products (AC9TDE2K02). They have explored movement through play. They have not yet described the relationship between forces, material properties and function, or connected these to design decisions in a product or system.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe how forces (push, pull, gravity, buoyancy) and the properties of materials (strength, flexibility, weight) affect the function of products and systems.
elaborations: researching how First Nations Australians consider buoyant forces as they select materials for watercraft, for example making bark or dugout canoes
looking at models to identify how materials are used and movement is created, for example in the design of a toy with wheels or moving parts

exploring through play how movement can be started by combining materials and using forces, for example releasing a wound rubber band to propel a model boat, how different materials may impact a marble roll speed, or how various surfaces from carpet to grass to concrete might affect a robot's movement
deconstructing a product or system to identify how motion and forces affect performance, for example in a puppet such as a Japanese bunraku puppet or a model windmill with moving sails

identifying engineered systems and experimenting with available local materials, tools and equipment to solve problems, for example designing a container or parachute that will keep an egg intact when dropped from a height; a pop-up card; a tower; or a vehicle

nodes.label: Forces that act on products and systems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name the forces acting on a product or system and describe what each force does
criteria: Names at least two forces and describes what each does
Connects a named force to a product or system context
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot name the forces acting on a product cannot proceed to N2's material-property explanations or N3's combined explanation — describing how materials interact with forces requires knowing which forces are at play.

width.minimum: Name at least two forces (e.g. push, pull, gravity, buoyancy) and describe what each one does in a product or system context
width.typical: Describe the forces acting in different products and systems — pushing, pulling, gravity acting on a falling or supported object, buoyancy keeping a watercraft afloat; explain how each force affects what the product or system does
wider: Research how First Nations Australians consider buoyant forces when selecting materials for watercraft such as bark or dugout canoes — examine how understanding of buoyancy informs material choice
Explore how forces interact in a puppet system (e.g. a Japanese bunraku puppet) — identify which forces act on each part and how designers use them to control movement

nodes.label: Material properties and their role in function
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify material properties (strength, flexibility, weight, buoyancy) and explain how each affects what a product or system can do
criteria: Names at least two material properties correctly
Explains how one property affects the function of a specific product
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot connect material properties to function cannot complete the N3 integration — the combined explanation (force + property → function) requires both building blocks.

width.minimum: Name at least two material properties and explain how one of them affects the function of a product
width.typical: Describe how material properties (strength, flexibility, weight, hardness, buoyancy) affect function across different products; explain why a designer would choose a material with specific properties for a given purpose
wider: Investigate how different surface materials (carpet, grass, concrete) affect a robot's or vehicle's movement — describe how the interaction between material properties and forces determines performance

Compare how materials from different cultural contexts (e.g. bark, bamboo, plantation timber, synthetic materials) have different properties and how those properties make them suited to different design applications

modes.reason: Students readily connect material properties to obvious cases (metal is strong) but struggle to apply the concept when the relevant property is less obvious (e.g. flexibility in a parachute, weight in a toy with moving parts). More product contexts surface the range of relevant properties.

nodes.label: How forces and materials together determine function
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how the interaction between forces and material properties determines whether a product or system functions as intended
criteria: Names at least one force and one material property in the same explanation
Explains how both contribute to the product or system functioning as intended

width.minimum: Describe one product or system and explain how both a force and a material property work together to make it function (e.g. a rubber band releases stored force because the material is elastic)
width.typical: Describe how forces and material properties interact in a range of products and systems (a model with wheels, a parachute, a container protecting an object, a windmill with moving sails); explain how changing the material or the force would change the function
wider: Deconstruct a product or system (e.g. a model windmill, a pop-up card, a parachute) to identify all forces and material properties at work — explain how the design coordinates them to achieve the intended function

Design and test a container or parachute that keeps an egg intact when dropped — use observations about forces (gravity, air resistance) and material properties to explain why the design works or fails

modes.reason: The coordination of forces and material properties into a functional explanation is the descriptor's core demand. Students who understand each concept separately often struggle to describe them as an interactive system. This node is where the building blocks from nodes 1 and 2 come together.

Students tend to converge on a single product type when reasoning about forces and materials. Working across different product types — moving toys, watercraft, containers, structures — builds a more generalisable explanatory framework.

descriptors.title: Producing food and fibre
descriptors.description: describe the ways of producing food and fibre
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore how plants and animals are grown for food, clothing and shelter (AC9TDE2K03). They have encountered food and fibre production at an exploratory level. They have not yet described production methods, compared different production systems, or examined tools and technologies used in food and fibre production.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe the ways food and fibre are produced, including tools, equipment and procedures used to support plant and animal production.
elaborations: researching food and fibre production techniques and technologies developed by First Nations Australians, such as burning, tilling, planting, transplanting, watering, irrigating, weeding, thinning, cropping, storing and trading food

describing tools, equipment and procedures to improve plant and animal production, for example when growing vegetables in the school garden and producing environments such as a glasshouse (protected cropping) or animal housing including safe chicken shelters
comparing farming methods for food in Australia and a country in Asia, for example the use of different types of plants and animals and how diverse technologies are used to produce them

researching how animal fibres (for example wool, alpaca) and plant fibres (for example timber, cotton, bamboo) are produced in Australia, for example how production of plantation timbers may be different from bamboo production

nodes.label: Methods of food production
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe at least two methods used to produce food and explain what each involves
criteria: Names at least two food production methods
Describes what is involved in at least one method (tools, procedures, environment)

width.minimum: Describe at least two food production methods (e.g. growing vegetables, raising livestock, fishing) and explain what each involves
width.typical: Describe a range of food production methods in Australia — plant-based (crops, vegetables, orchards) and animal-based (livestock, dairy, seafood); explain what tools, equipment and procedures are involved in each
wider: Research food and fibre production techniques developed by First Nations Australians — including burning, tilling, planting, transplanting, watering, weeding, thinning, cropping, storing and trading — and describe how these methods support sustainable production
Compare farming methods for food in Australia and a country in Asia — describe how different plants and animals are used and how diverse technologies support their production

nodes.label: Methods of fibre production
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how animal and plant fibres are produced and name examples of each
criteria: Names at least one animal fibre and one plant fibre correctly
Describes the production process for at least one fibre type

width.minimum: Name one animal fibre and one plant fibre and describe how each is produced
width.typical: Describe how animal fibres (wool, alpaca) and plant fibres (timber, cotton, bamboo) are produced in Australia; explain what tools, equipment and production environments are involved; compare at least two fibre types
wider: Research how production of plantation timbers differs from bamboo production — compare growth rates, land use, harvesting methods and sustainability implications
Investigate how First Nations Australians produced and used plant and animal fibres — describe production methods and how they differ from contemporary industrial fibre production

modes.reason: Students often know that wool comes from sheep but have thin understanding of the production process — shearing, processing, spinning. Fibre types vary significantly in production method, and examining both animal and plant fibres prevents students from over-generalising from one example.

nodes.label: Tools, environments and production systems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how tools, equipment and production environments (e.g. school garden, glasshouse, animal housing) are used to improve food or fibre production
criteria: Names at least one production environment and explains its purpose
Connects tools or equipment to a specific production improvement

width.minimum: Describe one production environment (e.g. a school garden, a glasshouse, a chicken shelter) and explain how it improves production
width.typical: Describe how different tools, equipment and production environments support plant and animal production; explain how each improves yield, safety or sustainability; include examples from both plant-based and animal-based production
wider: Design and describe a simple production environment (e.g. a school vegetable garden, a seed propagation setup) — identify what tools and procedures would improve production and justify choices
Investigate how protected cropping (glasshouses) changes what can be produced and where — compare to outdoor farming and discuss what factors influence the choice of production environment

modes.reason: Describing production systems integrates knowledge of methods (node 1 and 2) with the tools and environments that make those methods effective. Students who understand methods separately often do not connect them to the infrastructure that supports production — this node is where that integration happens.

descriptors.title: Food selection and healthy eating
descriptors.description: describe the ways food can be selected and prepared for healthy eating
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore how food can be selected and prepared for healthy eating (AC9TDE2K04). They have explored food selection at a general level. They have not yet described specific selection criteria, examined food technologies for health and safety, or compared fresh and processed foods by nutritional content.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe the ways food can be selected and prepared for healthy eating, including how food technologies support food safety and nutrient retention and how sensory properties inform selection.
elaborations: exploring how First Nations Australians consider the nutrient content of seasonal foods as a means of maintaining a balanced diet

recognising the benefits food technologies provide for health and food safety and to ensure that a wide variety of food is available and can be prepared for healthy eating, for example pasteurisation of milk for food safety and freezing of vegetables to retain nutrients and reduce food waste

exploring the differences between fresh food and processed food by researching nutrient content of fresh food using a nutrition calculator app and examining nutrition information labels on processed foods for nutritional values

considering creative ways foods can be prepared for maximum taste and appeal, for example locating and discussing images online that show colourful or fun ways to present food that might encourage healthy eating
describing foods using the senses, for example describing the colour, aroma, sound, texture and taste of the ingredients in a salad or stir-fry and how our senses influence what we select to eat

nodes.label: How food is selected for healthy eating
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe factors that influence food selection for healthy eating, including nutrient content and sensory properties
criteria: Names at least one factor used when selecting food for healthy eating
Explains how that factor guides a selection decision
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who only think of taste or appearance as selection criteria cannot apply nutritional reasoning when evaluating food technologies (N2) or comparing fresh vs processed foods (N3) — the selection framework must be broader than personal preference before technology comparisons are meaningful.

width.minimum: Describe at least one factor used to select food for healthy eating (e.g. nutrient content, freshness, sensory appeal) and explain how it guides selection
width.typical: Describe how nutrient content, seasonal availability, sensory properties (colour, aroma, texture, taste) and cultural context influence food selection for healthy eating; apply at least one method of assessing nutritional value (e.g. nutrition label, nutrition app)
wider: Explore how First Nations Australians consider the nutrient content of seasonal foods to maintain a balanced diet — investigate examples of seasonal food knowledge and discuss how this supports healthy eating
Use a nutrition calculator app to compare the nutrient content of several fresh foods — identify which nutrients are present and discuss how the data informs healthy selection decisions

modes.reason: Students typically focus on taste or 'what looks good' as selection criteria. Examining different selection factors — nutrients, seasonal availability, cultural practice — builds a more complete understanding of what healthy selection means and why it varies across contexts.

nodes.label: Food technologies and their role in health and safety
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe what food technologies do and explain how they support food safety, nutrient retention or food availability
criteria: Names at least one food technology and describes what it does
Connects the technology to food safety, nutrient retention or food availability

width.minimum: Describe one food technology (e.g. pasteurisation, freezing, refrigeration) and explain what it does for food safety or nutrient retention
width.typical: Describe how food technologies (pasteurisation, freezing, refrigeration, packaging) support food safety, retain nutrients and make a wide variety of food available; explain how each technology addresses a specific food challenge
wider: Investigate how freezing vegetables to retain nutrients reduces food waste — compare frozen vegetables with fresh and processed equivalents and discuss what the technology preserves and what it changes

Explore how food technologies used in Australia and an Asian country differ — compare preservation and preparation technologies and discuss why different technologies are used in different food cultures

nodes.label: Fresh vs processed food and preparation choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe differences between fresh and processed foods in terms of nutritional value and explain how preparation choices affect healthy eating
criteria: Describes at least one nutritional difference between a fresh and processed food
Explains one preparation choice that makes food healthier or more appealing

width.minimum: Describe one difference between a fresh food and a processed version of the same food, and explain one preparation choice that supports healthy eating
width.typical: Compare fresh and processed foods using nutrition labels and apps; describe differences in nutritional value; explain how preparation methods (e.g. cooking techniques, presentation choices) affect taste, appeal and healthiness
wider: Explore creative ways food can be prepared for maximum taste and appeal — locate and discuss examples of colourful or inventive food presentation that encourages healthy eating choices

Compare the nutritional information from a nutrition calculator app for a fresh ingredient versus a processed product using the same ingredient — analyse what the processing has added or removed and discuss what this means for healthy eating

modes.reason: Comparing fresh and processed foods integrates selection knowledge (node 1) with technology knowledge (node 2) — students must use both nutritional understanding and knowledge of food technologies to make sense of why processed and fresh foods differ. The comparison task is where these concepts come together.

descriptors.title: Explore needs and test materials
descriptors.description: explore needs or opportunities for designing, and test materials, components, tools, equipment and processes needed to create designed solutions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can generate and communicate design ideas through describing, drawing or modelling (AC9TDE2P01) and use materials, components, tools and equipment to safely make designed solutions (AC9TDE2P02). They have not yet explored needs systematically or tested materials for suitability before designing.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore needs or opportunities for designing, and test materials, components, tools, equipment and processes for suitability before creating designed solutions.
elaborations: exploring the designs and performance of models of First Nations Australians' watercraft, and the opportunities for their designs to inform the design of a floating toy

examining the production of local products, services and environments to enhance their own design ideas, for example discussing the processes and systems that might be used to distribute hot food to a large number of people at a community event

selecting and making judgements about appropriate joining techniques for materials to produce designs, prototypes, structures or working models, for example joining fabric, paper or cardboard in various ways

exploring and testing a range of materials under different conditions for suitability including sustainability considerations, for example the compostability of paper-based materials or the strength and durability of natural materials

exploring the different uses of materials in a range of products, including those from a country in Asia, to inform design decisions, for example in shelters, boats, handmade tools, baskets, wooden items, musical instruments, clothing and fabric

nodes.label: Identifying needs and design opportunities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe a need or opportunity that could be addressed through a designed solution
criteria: Identifies a specific need or opportunity (not just 'I want to make something')
Describes what a designed solution would need to do to address it
