nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify a specific design need cannot conduct purposeful material testing in N2 — testing without a design purpose produces observations but not selection reasoning.

width.minimum: Identify one need or opportunity and describe what kind of designed solution could address it
width.typical: Explore a range of needs and opportunities for designing (functional, community, environmental); describe what design opportunities each presents; examine existing products or services that address similar needs to inform design thinking
wider: Explore the designs and performance of models of First Nations Australians' watercraft — investigate the opportunity for their design principles to inform a new floating toy design
Examine local products and services (e.g. food distribution at a community event, school access features) and identify design opportunities for improvement, innovation or sustainability

nodes.label: Testing materials for suitability
nodes.checkpoint: Students can test materials under relevant conditions and describe what the test revealed about suitability for a design purpose
criteria: Conducts a test on at least one material
Describes what the test revealed about the material's suitability for the design purpose
nodes.hinge_reason: Material test results are the primary input to N3 decisions about what is needed for the design solution — students who conduct no genuine testing arrive at N3 without evidence for their component and process choices.

width.minimum: Test at least one material for a specific property relevant to a design purpose (e.g. strength, flexibility, compostability) and describe what the test revealed
width.typical: Test a range of materials under different conditions for suitability — including sustainability considerations (compostability, durability of natural materials); describe what each test reveals and use results to make material selection judgements
wider: Explore materials from a range of cultural contexts (e.g. shelters, boats, handmade tools, baskets from an Asian country) — test or compare equivalent materials and describe how their properties make them suited to different design applications

Test joining techniques (fabric, paper, cardboard) and evaluate which is strongest, most flexible or most appropriate for the design purpose — explain how the testing process informed the selection decision

modes.reason: Students often test only one property (e.g. strength) without considering that the relevant property depends on the design purpose. Testing across different material types and properties — including sustainability properties like compostability — builds a more complete understanding of what 'suitable' means.

nodes.label: Testing components, tools and processes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can test components, tools or processes and describe what testing reveals about which are needed for a designed solution
criteria: Tests at least one component, tool or process
Connects the test finding to a specific design decision

width.minimum: Test one tool, component or process and describe how the test informed a design decision
width.typical: Test a range of components, tools, equipment and processes for suitability; use test results alongside material testing to make decisions about what is needed to create the designed solution; document test findings
wider: Test and compare joining techniques (adhesives, stitching, fasteners) for a specific design purpose — evaluate which technique best balances strength, aesthetics and ease of use, and justify the choice
Explore how virtual reality or simulations can be used to test assembling processes before physical production — discuss what testing digitally reveals and what it does not

modes.reason: Testing components and processes alongside materials (node 2) into a coherent set of design decisions is the integration challenge. Students often treat material testing and tool/process testing as separate activities — this node asks them to use all test findings together to inform what the solution will need.

descriptors.title: Generate and communicate design ideas
descriptors.description: generate and communicate design ideas and decisions using appropriate attributions, technical terms and graphical representation techniques, including using digital tools
descriptors.knowledge: Students can generate and communicate design ideas through describing, drawing or modelling, including using digital tools (AC9TDE2P01). They have communicated design ideas informally. They have not yet used technical terms, annotated diagrams, attributions, or more formal graphical representation techniques.
descriptors.endpoint: Students generate and communicate design ideas and decisions using appropriate technical terms, attributions and graphical representation techniques, including annotated diagrams and digital tools.
elaborations: visualising innovative design ideas by producing thumbnail sketches, models and labelled drawings to explain features and modifications, for example drawing one or more designs for a machine to collect waste, and including labels and descriptions to explain materials used, their properties and the intended function of components or the whole system

planning, sharing and documenting creative designs, ideas and processes using digital tools and appropriate terms and privacy considerations, for example a class blog or collaborative document that has been selectively shared with peers

communicating design ideas using annotated diagrams, for example labelling a diagram for a pushcart with technical terms and explanations about components such as the chassis, axle, wheels and steering
generating design ideas for solutions using Safety by Design principles, for example designing communication that is accessible for all parents and carers

nodes.label: Generating design ideas through sketching and modelling
nodes.checkpoint: Students can produce multiple design ideas for a problem using thumbnail sketches or models
criteria: Produces at least two visibly different design ideas
Each sketch or model shows enough detail to understand what it proposes
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who produce only one design idea arrive at N2 and N3 with nothing to annotate or communicate distinctively — the communication tasks assume multiple ideas have been generated.

width.minimum: Produce at least two thumbnail sketches or models for a design problem, with enough detail to distinguish the ideas
width.typical: Produce multiple thumbnail sketches, labelled drawings and/or models for design problems; include features and modifications in each idea; explore ideas for different design problems
wider: Generate design ideas inspired by First Nations Australians' watercraft or other traditional designs — describe how prior design knowledge can inform new ideas

Generate design ideas for solutions using Safety by Design principles — produce sketches that show how the design ensures accessibility for all users (e.g. all parents and carers can access communication)

nodes.label: Using technical terms and annotations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can label a design drawing using appropriate technical terms and explain what each component is and does
criteria: Uses at least two technical terms correctly in annotations
Annotations explain function, not just name the part
nodes.hinge_reason: Technical annotation and attributions are required components of the N3 digital communication task — students who have not consolidated annotation practice cannot produce the complete communication the descriptor requires.

width.minimum: Label at least one design drawing with technical terms for two or more components, with a brief explanation of each
width.typical: Communicate design ideas using annotated diagrams with technical terms for all major components; include labels and descriptions explaining materials used, their properties, and the intended function of components or the whole system
wider: Annotate a design for a more complex system (e.g. a pushcart with chassis, axle, wheels and steering) using technical terms for each component — explain not just what each part is but why it was designed that way

Research and apply technical terms from a related design field (e.g. engineering, textile design) to annotate a student design — discuss how technical language helps communicate design decisions to different audiences

modes.reason: Technical vocabulary in design communication needs fluency — students who can label a design correctly and consistently are better positioned for the more complex communication tasks in subsequent years. Precision and accuracy in annotation matters more than breadth of context here.

nodes.label: Communicating and sharing design ideas with attributions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can share and document design ideas using digital tools, including appropriate attributions and privacy considerations
criteria: Design communication includes technical terms and at least one attribution
Digital tool has been used to share or document the design

width.minimum: Share a design idea using a digital tool, with at least one attribution for an idea or reference that informed it
width.typical: Plan, share and document creative design ideas using digital tools; apply appropriate technical terms; include attributions for ideas drawn from other sources; apply privacy considerations when sharing collaboratively (e.g. class blog, shared document)
wider: Document a design process using a class blog or collaborative digital document — include annotations, attributions and reflections on design decisions shared selectively with peers
Communicate a design idea for a cultural context beyond the student's own experience — discuss what additional research and attribution is needed to communicate the design respectfully and accurately

modes.reason: Communicating a complete design idea using digital tools, technical terms, annotations and attributions together is the integration point. Each element has been practised separately — this node is where students coordinate them into a coherent design communication.

descriptors.title: Select and use materials safely
descriptors.description: select and use materials, components, tools, equipment and techniques to safely make designed solutions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use materials, components, tools, equipment and techniques to safely make designed solutions (AC9TDE2P02). They have used materials and tools in a supervised context. They have not yet selected materials with justified reasons, considered environmental impact across the production process, or used appropriate technologies terminology to describe procedures.
descriptors.endpoint: Students select and use materials, components, tools, equipment and techniques to safely make designed solutions, with consideration of environmental impact and using appropriate terminology to describe procedures.
elaborations: exploring ways of joining, connecting and assembling components that ensure success including the impact digital tools have on these processes, for example using virtual reality or simulations to experience assembling materials or using tools
using tools and equipment accurately when measuring, marking and cutting, for example when creating a template or pattern, measuring ingredients in a recipe or preparing a garden bed for sowing seeds
explaining the importance of safe, responsible, inclusive and cooperative work practices when designing and making, for example when handling sharp equipment such as knives and scissors

selecting and using materials, components, tools, equipment and processes with consideration of the environmental impact at each stage of the production process, for example considering how packaging and offcuts could be recycled or used for other purposes before choosing materials for a project
using appropriate technologies terms to describe and share with other students the procedures and techniques for making, for example how to safely make an engineered solution such as a robotic device

nodes.label: Selecting materials with reasons
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select materials and components for a design purpose and give reasons for their choices that reference material properties or sustainability
criteria: Names at least two materials chosen for the design
Gives at least one reason for each choice that references a property or sustainability factor
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who select materials without reasoning about properties make production decisions that can compromise function and safety — arbitrary selection cannot be remedied in N2 and N3 because material choices are already locked in.

width.minimum: Select at least two materials for a design task and give one reason for each choice (referencing a property or sustainability consideration)
width.typical: Select materials, components and joining techniques for design tasks with reasons; consider environmental impact in selections — for example whether packaging and offcuts can be recycled; explain selections using technologies terms
wider: Select materials with explicit sustainability consideration — compare materials by compostability, recyclability and durability before choosing; document the selection reasoning

Explore material choices from products made in an Asian country (e.g. bamboo, different timber types, natural fibres) — compare to materials typically available locally and discuss how material availability shapes design decisions

modes.reason: Students often select materials based on appearance or familiarity rather than properties relevant to function and sustainability. Scaffolding the selection reasoning (identify the design requirement → identify which property matters → check the material has that property) builds deliberate material selection practice.

nodes.label: Safe, responsible and cooperative making practices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can demonstrate safe, responsible and inclusive work practices when using tools and equipment
criteria: Applies at least two safe work practices without prompting
Uses at least one tool accurately (measuring, marking or cutting to a specified dimension)
nodes.hinge_reason: Safe work practices are a non-negotiable gate for all physical making — students who have not consolidated safe handling cannot proceed to production contexts in N3. This is a safety prerequisite, not a quality issue.

width.minimum: Demonstrate at least two safe work practices when using tools or equipment (e.g. correct grip, checking workspace is clear, appropriate handling of sharp equipment)
width.typical: Explain and apply safe, responsible, inclusive and cooperative work practices across different making contexts; use tools and equipment accurately when measuring, marking and cutting; explain why each safety practice matters
wider: Describe the safety practices relevant to making a specific engineered solution (e.g. a robotic device) — explain how safety practices change when tools and materials become more complex
Explore how digital tools (virtual reality, simulations) can be used to practise assembly before physical making — discuss what safety benefits this approach offers and what it does not replace

modes.reason: Safe work practices require habitual, precise application. Consolidation — consistent practice across making tasks, with feedback — is what builds reliable safety behaviour. Breadth of context matters less than accuracy and consistency of practice.

nodes.label: Using technologies terminology to describe procedures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the procedures and techniques used in making, using appropriate technologies terms
criteria: Uses at least two technologies terms correctly in context
Procedural description is clear enough for another student to follow

width.minimum: Use at least two technologies terms correctly when describing a making procedure to another student
width.typical: Use appropriate technologies terms to describe and share procedures and techniques for making across different design contexts; include terms for materials, tools, components and processes
wider: Document a making procedure for a complex product (e.g. an engineered robotic device or a textile item) using technologies terms and steps clear enough for another student to follow
Create a visual or digital guide to a making procedure using appropriate terminology — evaluate whether the guide is clear enough for a peer who has not done the task before

modes.reason: Technologies terminology needs to be built across different materials, tools and making contexts. Students who only use terms in one context (e.g. woodwork) may not transfer them to textiles or food technology. Repertoire across making domains is the target.

descriptors.title: Evaluate with design criteria
descriptors.description: use given or co-developed design criteria including sustainability to evaluate design ideas and solutions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can evaluate the success of design ideas and solutions based on personal preferences and including sustainability (AC9TDE2P03). They have evaluated based on personal judgement. They have not yet used explicit design criteria as the basis for evaluation or co-developed criteria with others.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use given or co-developed design criteria — including sustainability — to evaluate design ideas and solutions, with reasons grounded in the criteria.
elaborations: developing design criteria with others including considering universal design principles to address social sustainability, for example a criterion that specifies flexible or intuitive use or low physical effort
using design criteria to evaluate, revise and select design ideas, for example when designing an e-textile toy for a young child to ensure it will be safe

comparing the amount of waste that would be produced from different design ideas and the potential for recycling waste, for example exploring the choice of materials to construct a toy and whether these materials are repairable or able to be recycled once the toy breaks or is no longer wanted

reflecting on how well their designed solution meets design criteria, such as ensuring safety and wellbeing of users and meeting the needs of communities or different cultures, for example reviewing and discussing the choice of fabrics used to make re-usable bags and how they could be made more appealing to all cultural groups by considering modifications to style

nodes.label: Understanding design criteria as evaluation tools
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what design criteria are and describe what a solution would need to do to meet a given criterion
criteria: Explains what at least two criteria require of a solution
Distinguishes between criteria and solution (criteria state what the solution must do; they are not the solution itself)
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot interpret what a criterion requires of a solution cannot co-develop meaningful criteria in N2 or evaluate against them in N3 — the evaluation task requires correctly reading the criteria first.

width.minimum: Read a set of given design criteria and explain in plain language what a solution must do to satisfy at least two of them
width.typical: Read and interpret design criteria for different design problems; explain what each criterion requires of a solution; distinguish between criteria that are met and criteria that are not met for a given solution
wider: Examine design criteria that include universal design principles (flexible use, low physical effort, intuitive use) — explain what each principle means as a design requirement and how it addresses social sustainability
Compare two sets of criteria for the same problem — discuss how different criteria lead to different design priorities and potentially different solutions

nodes.label: Co-developing design criteria
nodes.checkpoint: Students can contribute to developing design criteria with others, including at least one criterion related to sustainability
criteria: Contributes at least one criterion with a stated reason
The contributed criterion addresses something a solution must do, not a preference

width.minimum: Contribute at least one criterion to a co-developed set, explaining why it matters for the design problem
width.typical: Co-develop design criteria with others for a design problem; include criteria addressing function, safety, sustainability and user needs; explain the reasoning behind each criterion
wider: Develop design criteria that include a social sustainability criterion addressing accessibility for different user groups — explain how this criterion reflects universal design thinking

Develop criteria for a product that will be evaluated by users from different cultural backgrounds — discuss how criteria might need to reflect diverse needs and what this reveals about how criteria are never fully neutral

modes.reason: Students who only develop criteria for one type of problem (e.g. a toy) may not see that criteria development is always contextual. Developing criteria across different problem types and user groups builds the habit of thinking from the user's perspective rather than the designer's preferences.

nodes.label: Evaluating ideas and solutions against criteria
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate a design idea or solution against criteria — including sustainability — and provide reasons grounded in the criteria
criteria: States whether each criterion is met with a reason
At least one criterion involves sustainability
Evaluation references the solution's features, not just personal preference

width.minimum: Evaluate one design idea or solution against at least two criteria and state whether each criterion is met, with a reason for each judgement
width.typical: Evaluate design ideas and solutions against criteria including sustainability across different design contexts; use evaluation to revise and select between design ideas; reflect on how well the final solution meets the criteria
wider: Compare the waste produced by different design ideas and the potential for recycling — use sustainability criteria to evaluate and select between design ideas based on material choices

Evaluate a designed solution against criteria that include safety, sustainability and community/cultural appropriateness — discuss cases where criteria compete (e.g. a more sustainable material is less durable) and how to reason through trade-offs

modes.reason: Evaluating against criteria requires criterion-by-criterion reasoning, not an overall impression. Scaffolding the process prevents students from simply stating a preference. The reasoning move (identify criterion → check solution → state match/gap → give reason) needs to become habitual.

Evaluation integrates criteria knowledge (node 1), co-developed criteria (node 2), and knowledge of materials and sustainability (AC9TDE4K01, K02) into a practical judgement. The coordination of multiple knowledge sources in an evaluation task is the descriptor's full demand.

descriptors.title: Sequence collaborative production
descriptors.description: sequence steps to individually and collaboratively make designed solutions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can sequence steps for making designed solutions cooperatively (AC9TDE2P04). They have sequenced steps in a cooperative context. They have not yet worked with explicit planning tools (timelines, spreadsheets, flowcharts), managed time and resource allocation, or understood mass production processes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students sequence steps to individually and collaboratively make designed solutions, using planning tools to record steps and manage time and resource allocation.
elaborations: determining planning processes as a class, for example recording when parts of a project need to be completed on a timeline, in a spreadsheet, calendar or list

discussing the importance of managing time and resource allocation throughout production, for example discussing the roles different people might take in a team and identifying the tasks they will complete and the resources they will each need

identifying the steps in a mass production process, for example drawing a flowchart or making a video recording of a procedure for packing identical boxes of food for community members in need, where each student in a group has a separate task as part of the production process

nodes.label: Planning and recording production steps
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a production sequence and record it using a planning tool such as a timeline, list or flowchart
criteria: Steps are recorded in a logical sequence using a planning tool
The sequence includes enough steps to complete the making task without missing key stages
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot record a production sequence cannot contribute to the role and resource allocation in N2 — planning tools are the shared artefact that makes role coordination possible.

width.minimum: Record the steps for making a designed solution in sequence using at least one planning tool (e.g. a list, a timeline, a simple flowchart)
width.typical: Determine and record production steps using planning tools — timelines, spreadsheets, calendars or lists; include when parts of the project need to be completed; use planning tools for both individual and collaborative tasks
wider: Create a flowchart for a mass production process — for example, packing identical food boxes where each student has a separate task; identify decision points and parallel steps in the sequence

Draw a flowchart or record a video of a procedure with a fixed sequence (e.g. packing boxes for community members in need) — evaluate whether the recorded steps are clear and complete enough for someone else to follow

modes.reason: Students who only plan sequences for simple personal tasks may not understand how planning tools scale to more complex production. Experiencing planning for both individual making and multi-role collaborative production builds a more complete understanding of sequencing as a management tool.

nodes.label: Managing time and resource allocation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify roles and resources needed in a collaborative production task and explain how these are managed to complete the task
criteria: Names at least two roles in a collaborative task
Identifies the resources each role needs to complete its tasks
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot reason about role dependencies and resource needs cannot coordinate a collaborative production in N3 — they will block other roles or run out of resources mid-task.

width.minimum: In a collaborative making task, identify at least two roles and the resources each role needs; contribute to a plan that allocates tasks
width.typical: Discuss the importance of managing time and resources throughout production; identify roles different people might take in a team; map tasks to roles and identify the resources each needs; contribute to a shared plan
wider: Plan a collaborative production event (e.g. food distribution for a community event) — identify all roles, resources and the sequence of tasks; discuss how delays or resource shortages in one role affect others
Reflect on a completed collaborative task — identify where time or resource management broke down and propose how the plan could be improved for next time

modes.reason: Resource and role allocation requires students to reason about dependencies — what does each person need, and what happens if a resource is unavailable? Scaffolding this reasoning (identify role → identify resource needed → identify what could block progress) builds production planning thinking rather than just task-listing.

nodes.label: Individual and collaborative production sequences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can sequence steps for both individual and collaborative production tasks and explain how collaborative sequences differ from individual ones
criteria: Follows a planned production sequence to completion
Describes at least one difference between individual and collaborative sequencing

width.minimum: Complete a production task — individually or collaboratively — following a planned sequence, and describe at least one way the collaborative sequence required coordination that an individual sequence did not
width.typical: Sequence and follow production steps for both individual and collaborative tasks; explain how collaborative sequencing requires task allocation, timing coordination and role communication that individual sequencing does not; use a planning tool to manage the process
wider: Identify the steps in a mass production process — each student has a separate task in a production line (e.g. packing food boxes); discuss how the sequence must be coordinated so the whole production runs efficiently

Compare an individual production sequence with a collaborative one for the same product — identify which steps are divided, which are parallel and which must be sequential regardless of how many people are involved

modes.reason: This node integrates planning tools (node 1) with role and resource management (node 2) into a completed collaborative production experience. The integration challenge is coordinating steps, roles and resources simultaneously in real time — the coordination is the learning.

descriptors.title: Competing factors in design
descriptors.description: Explain how people in design and technologies occupations consider competing factors including sustainability in the design of products, services and environments
descriptors.knowledge: Students can examine design and technologies occupations and factors including sustainability that impact on the design of products, services and environments (AC9TDE4K01). They have identified that designers consider multiple factors. They have not yet explained how competing factors are weighed against each other — the tension between them and how practitioners resolve it.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how people in design and technologies occupations weigh competing factors including sustainability when designing products, services and environments, and identify examples of innovative solutions that resolve such tensions.
elaborations: investigating how First Nations Australians have long considered competing factors especially those related to sustainability in the design of fish harvesting technologies, for example fish traps and fish poisons that allow for selective harvesting and release of bycatch, as compared with high-yield, non-selective harvesting practices such as trawling

describing the impact and sustainability implications of designed products, services or environments on local, regional and global communities, for example the emergence of small businesses that are recycling materials, such as plastic tags and bottle tops into prosthetics

explaining the importance of aesthetics, function and sustainability in product design, for example a textile product that gives ultraviolet protection and is appealing; an odour-fighting wool fabric that minimises washing; a motor that moves a vehicle and uses a sustainable power source; a modification to a home to reduce environmental impact; restoring a natural environment and enabling low-impact access for the public such as boardwalks in fragile wet heath or swamp ecosystems

identifying the components of a service that contribute to its success and assessing potential risk or failure, for example a community service announcement to communicate a message in the school or to a wide audience; a service that manages an aspect of the environment such as Clean Up Australia Day in different communities
considering how engineers resolve competing factors to produce innovative solutions, for example experimenting with novel ideas such as biomimicry to engineer a solution such as a soft robotic device

considering how Safety by Design principles have been used in the design of products, services or environments, for example considering how prevention, protection and proactive change can be used to improve safety of designed solutions

nodes.label: What competing factors means in design
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that designers must weigh multiple factors that can pull in different directions, and name at least three factors that commonly compete
criteria: Names at least three factors that designers must consider
Explains at least one example where two factors conflict with each other
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify competing factors have no framework for design decision-making — every downstream capability (P01 investigation, P04 criteria negotiation, P03 material selection) requires reasoning through trade-offs. Without this, design decisions reduce to personal preference.

width.minimum: Name at least three factors a designer must consider (e.g. cost, sustainability, function, aesthetics, safety) and give one example where two factors pull in opposite directions
width.typical: Explain that design involves balancing competing factors that cannot all be maximised simultaneously; identify and describe how specific factors (aesthetics, function, sustainability, safety, cost) compete in a familiar product or service context
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians considered competing factors in designing fish harvesting technologies — comparing selective harvesting techniques (fish traps, fish poisons allowing bycatch release) with high-yield non-selective methods like trawling
Investigate how Safety by Design principles (prevention, protection, proactive change) compete with other design factors such as cost and ease of use in a product or service context
Examine how engineers use biomimicry to resolve competing factors — finding a natural solution where function, sustainability and materials performance are already optimised

modes.reason: Students tend to treat factors as independent checklists rather than tensions. Multiple design contexts — each featuring a different pair of competing factors — help students see that the conflict between factors is the design problem, not just a constraint list.

nodes.label: Sustainability as a competing factor
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how sustainability considerations compete with other design priorities and identify design decisions that resolve this tension
criteria: Identifies a specific design decision where sustainability was weighed against another factor
Explains what the designer chose and why

width.minimum: Describe one product, service or environment where sustainability was weighed against another factor, and explain what design decision was made
width.typical: Explain the sustainability implications of design decisions on local, regional and global communities; describe how designers resolve tension between sustainability and other priorities in at least two contexts (e.g. materials, energy, waste)
wider: Investigate the emergence of small businesses recycling materials (e.g. plastic tags and bottle tops into prosthetics) — explaining how they resolved the competition between cost, material availability, and sustainability

Evaluate a household product designed to reduce environmental impact (e.g. a solar-powered motor, a water-harvesting system, a boardwalk through fragile wetland) — identifying which competing factors the designer prioritised and which were deprioritised

Investigate the sustainability of a community service (e.g. Clean Up Australia Day in different communities) — assessing what factors contribute to its success and what sustainability risks or failures could occur

modes.reason: Sustainability is often treated as self-evidently good — students need contexts where it genuinely competes with something valuable (cost, performance, convenience) to understand it as a trade-off that designers actively negotiate rather than a principle they simply adopt.

descriptors.title: Electrical energy transformations
descriptors.description: Explain how electrical energy can be transformed into movement, sound or light in a product or system
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe how forces and the properties of materials affect function in a product or system (AC9TDE4K02). They understand that materials have properties that affect how products work. They have not yet connected electrical energy specifically to output transformations — movement, sound, or light — or worked with circuits as systems.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how electrical energy is transformed into movement, sound or light in products and systems, and can identify the components needed to control these transformations.
elaborations: investigating how automated, labour-saving photovoltaic systems are expected to provide opportunities for First Nations Australians to expand their aquaculture industries in coastal regions of northern Australia
explaining how sun tracking of solar panels assists renewable energy production in communities classified as remote

describing the process needed to carefully plan and select components for a system to perform a specific task, for example planning the arrangement of switches, light globes and a power source in a lighting design

producing models using materials, tools and equipment to show how to control movement, sound or light, for example constructing an automaton, automation system or lifting system including a pulley to raise a bucket or toy

deconstructing a product or system to discover how movement, sound or light can be controlled, for example taking apart a torch or buzzer, or exploring circuit design in a security system and investigating the properties of materials to solve problems including the amount of light reflected from different surfaces to control a sensor

nodes.label: Electrical energy can be transformed into different outputs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that electrical energy can be transformed into movement, sound or light, and give an example of each
criteria: Names at least two different outputs of electrical energy transformation
Identifies the component that performs the transformation in at least one product
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify that electrical energy transforms into different outputs cannot reason about which components to select or arrange in N2 — the planning and control task in N2 requires knowing what transformation is needed.

width.minimum: Identify at least two different outputs that electrical energy can be transformed into (movement, sound, light) and name a product that performs each transformation
width.typical: Explain how electrical energy is transformed into movement, sound or light across a range of products; describe what component performs the transformation in each case (e.g. motor → movement, speaker → sound, LED → light)
wider: Investigate how automated photovoltaic (solar) systems transform electrical energy to control movement in aquaculture systems — explaining how this creates opportunities for First Nations Australians in coastal northern Australia
Deconstruct a torch or buzzer to identify the components and explain how each contributes to the energy transformation — tracing the path from power source to output
Investigate how sun-tracking solar panels use electrical energy to control movement, and how this improves renewable energy production efficiency in remote communities

modes.reason: Students commonly know that electricity 'powers' things but don't think of it as a transformation — energy changing form. Multiple products each showcasing a different transformation output (motor, LED, speaker) help students build the generalisation: electricity in, different form of energy out.

nodes.label: Planning and controlling a system to produce a specific output
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how components in a circuit or system are selected and arranged to produce and control a specific output (movement, sound or light)
criteria: Identifies the components needed for a circuit producing a specific output
Explains the role of each component in the system

width.minimum: Plan the components needed for a simple circuit that produces one specific output; explain the role of each component (power source, switch, output device)
width.typical: Plan and select components for a system to perform a specific task; explain how switches, power sources and output components work together; describe how the arrangement of components controls the output (e.g. controlling movement with a switch, varying light with different resistors)
wider: Construct or model a system that controls movement, sound or light — e.g. an automaton, a pulley-based lifting system, or a circuit in a security system — explaining how each component contributes to the overall output

Investigate the properties of materials that affect a circuit's output — for example, how the reflectivity of a surface affects a light sensor in a security system — connecting material properties to system performance

modes.reason: Component selection is a reasoning task — students must work backwards from the desired output to the components needed. The reasoning chain (what output is needed? → what component produces it? → what controls it? → what powers it?) prevents students from listing components without understanding their roles.

This node integrates individual component knowledge into a working system understanding. The switch, power source and output device must be understood as a coordinated system, not separate items — the integration act is designing for a specific, controlled output.

descriptors.title: Managed food and fibre production
descriptors.description: Explain how and why food and fibre are produced in managed environments
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe the ways of producing food and fibre (AC9TDE4K03). They understand that food and fibre come from different production systems. They have not yet explained how and why those environments are actively managed — the decisions, constraints, and sustainability practices behind production.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how food and fibre are produced in managed environments, including soil preparation, plant and animal selection, and supply chain processes, and why these management decisions are made.
elaborations: exploring how before colonisation, First Nations Australians lived in discrete communities that cared for, protected and sustainably harvested food and fibre resources, some of which are now cultivated to meet domestic and international demand, for example bunya nuts, macadamia and finger limes

investigating and experimenting with different tools, equipment and methods of preparing soil and the effect on soil quality and sustainability including conserving and recycling nutrients, for example building a food composting system, including mulch when designing a sustainable school vegetable garden or cropping area

describing the relationship between plant types and animal breeds and their environmental suitability when selecting suitable plants or animals for an environment, for example growing tropical fruits in northern Australia due to higher temperature, and raising sheep in the cooler regions of Australia

sequencing the process of converting on-farm food or fibre products into a product suitable for retail sale, for example creating a digital flowchart to record a paddock-to-plate supply chain, or the fibre-to-garment life cycle (fibre, yarn, fabric, garment)
visiting a farm or participating in a virtual tour to ask questions about how and why food and fibre are produced in that environment

nodes.label: Why food and fibre production requires active management
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why food and fibre production requires deliberate management decisions rather than just natural growth
criteria: Identifies at least two management decisions in food or fibre production
Explains why each decision is made — connecting it to a production goal or environmental constraint
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot explain why management decisions are made cannot sequence supply chain stages meaningfully in N2 — the 'why' of each stage (soil prep timing, harvest scheduling) requires understanding the management rationale, not just the step order.

width.minimum: Identify at least two management decisions made in a food or fibre production environment and explain why each decision is made
width.typical: Explain how soil preparation, plant selection and animal breed selection are management decisions made to match the environment; describe why specific plants or animals suit specific climates or regions — connecting environmental conditions to production outcomes
wider: Investigate how before colonisation, First Nations Australians managed food and fibre resources sustainably — including the cultivation of bunya nuts, macadamia and finger limes — and how some of these are now commercially cultivated to meet domestic and international demand

Compare tropical food production (northern Australia — higher temperature, tropical fruits) with temperate food production (cooler regions — sheep, cool-climate crops) — explaining how environment shapes management choices
Investigate and experiment with soil preparation methods (composting, mulching, nutrient cycling) and explain how each improves soil quality and production sustainability

modes.reason: Students tend to think of food production as natural rather than designed. Multiple managed environment contexts — different climates, different species, different management decisions — help students see production as a system of deliberate choices responsive to environmental constraints.

nodes.label: Supply chains — from production to retail
nodes.checkpoint: Students can sequence and explain the process of converting on-farm food or fibre products into a product suitable for retail sale
criteria: Sequences at least three stages in a food or fibre supply chain in correct order
Explains what happens at each stage

width.minimum: Identify at least three stages in a paddock-to-plate or fibre-to-garment supply chain and explain what happens at each stage
width.typical: Sequence the full supply chain for a food or fibre product — from production through processing to retail; explain what value is added at each stage and why each step is necessary; represent the chain visually (e.g. flowchart, diagram)
wider: Create a digital flowchart representing a paddock-to-plate supply chain for a locally grown product — annotating each stage with the management decisions and technologies involved
Sequence the fibre-to-garment life cycle (fibre → yarn → fabric → garment) and explain how decisions at each stage affect the sustainability and quality of the final product
Visit or virtually tour a farm and investigate how on-site decisions (breed selection, soil management, harvesting timing) affect the quality and quantity of product reaching the consumer

modes.reason: Students commonly know the end product and the raw material but cannot sequence the transformation steps. Tracing the supply chain as a connected sequence — where the output of each stage is the input of the next — makes the managed system legible as a designed process.

descriptors.title: Food characteristics and healthy eating
descriptors.description: Explain how the characteristics of foods influence selection and preparation for healthy eating
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe the ways food can be selected and prepared for healthy eating (AC9TDE4K04). They understand that food choices affect health. They have not yet explained how specific food characteristics (nutritional value, spoilage, preparation requirements, taste) drive selection and preparation decisions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how the characteristics of foods — nutritional value, spoilage, preparation requirements, taste — influence selection and preparation decisions for healthy eating.
elaborations: investigating how First Nations Australians have long selected and prepared foods for healthy eating, for example based on their nutritional value, availability, spoilage, preparation and processing requirements

using the Australian Dietary Guidelines to determine the recommended number of serves for an individual, for example describing and planning a healthy meal or lunchbox for a particular individual with recommended serving sizes to inform choices and then explaining the characteristics of the selected foods

experimenting with tools, equipment, ingredients and techniques to design and make food products or meals for selected groups for healthy eating taking into consideration environmental impacts and nutritional benefits, for example experimenting with preserving techniques including pickling, fermentation, air drying or sun drying and presenting information on the benefits for an audience
exploring a variety of tastes and how they may influence the selection or preparation of food, for example the sour, salty, sweet, spicy and umami flavours of many foods from countries across Asia
developing strategies to communicate healthy choices based on the Australian Dietary Guidelines, for example designing a website with food preparation tips for healthy eating for pre-teens
exploring the food service options of a local restaurant, café, fast food or takeaway establishment and identifying the food preparation skills needed to prepare food for healthy eating

nodes.label: Food characteristics that influence selection
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain how food characteristics — nutritional value, availability, spoilage, taste — influence which foods are selected for healthy eating
criteria: Names at least two food characteristics
Explains how each characteristic influences whether a food is selected for healthy eating
nodes.hinge_reason: Food selection reasoning in N1 cascades directly into N2 — if students cannot identify characteristics (spoilage risk, nutritional value) as the basis for selection, they cannot connect those same characteristics to preparation decisions. The two nodes share the same conceptual structure.

width.minimum: Identify at least two food characteristics and explain how each influences whether a food is selected for a healthy meal
width.typical: Explain how nutritional value, availability, spoilage risk, preparation requirements and taste each influence food selection; apply the Australian Dietary Guidelines to plan a healthy meal or lunchbox for a specific individual — explaining selection decisions in terms of food characteristics
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians have long selected foods based on nutritional value, seasonal availability, spoilage characteristics, and preparation requirements — exploring how this knowledge guided sustainable food choices over generations
Explore how flavour profiles (sour, salty, sweet, spicy, umami — particularly from Asian cuisines) influence food selection and preparation preferences across different cultural groups
Investigate how food service options at a local restaurant or café reflect food characteristic trade-offs — identifying how chefs balance nutrition, taste, availability and spoilage in menu design

modes.reason: Students tend to select foods based on taste preference and treat healthy eating as a rule set rather than a characteristic-based reasoning process. Multiple contexts — cultural traditions, dietary guidelines, food service — help students see food selection as applying a set of criteria to characteristics, not following a prescribed list.

nodes.label: Food characteristics that influence preparation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how food characteristics influence preparation methods and techniques
criteria: Identifies at least one food characteristic that determines how a food must be prepared
Explains the connection between the characteristic and the preparation method

width.minimum: Identify one food and explain how its characteristics (e.g. spoilage risk, texture, nutritional content) determine how it should be prepared
width.typical: Explain how different food characteristics — perishability, hygiene requirements, nutritional value, texture — determine preparation methods; apply this understanding to design a food product or meal that meets health and safety requirements
wider: Experiment with preservation techniques (pickling, fermentation, air drying, sun drying) and explain how each technique responds to specific food characteristics — connecting the preservation method to the characteristic being managed

Investigate work practices that reflect nutrition, hygiene and food safety considerations — explaining how washing produce, safe oil disposal, refrigeration of perishables, and allergen awareness each respond to a specific food characteristic
Explore the food service skills needed to prepare food for healthy eating in a restaurant or café context — identifying how preparation techniques vary with the food's characteristics

modes.reason: Students commonly follow preparation steps without connecting them to the food's characteristics. The reasoning chain — what characteristic does this food have? → what preparation risk or opportunity does that create? → what technique responds to it? — makes preparation decisions principled rather than procedural.

descriptors.title: Properties affect material use
descriptors.description: Explain how characteristics and properties of materials, systems, components, tools and equipment affect their use when producing designed solutions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe how forces and the properties of materials affect function in a product or system (AC9TDE4K02). They can describe material properties in relation to how products work. They have not yet explained how properties determine selection across a range of materials, systems, components, tools and equipment — or compared production approaches across different scales or cultural contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how the characteristics and properties of materials, systems, components, tools and equipment affect how they are selected and used when producing designed solutions.
elaborations: investigating how First Nations Australians have long used material science knowledge to identify materials and preparation techniques to meet performance needs, for example twining techniques of string and rope fibres to ensure suitability for use in wet, dry, freshwater and saltwater applications

identifying and describing the properties of materials for the design and construction of a household product or system to improve household sustainability, for example a product for storing harvested water or reducing energy consumption

describing the materials and systems used in public places and facilities that benefit the way people live, for example a community exercise environment, arts facility, water treatment plant or garbage collection service

comparing and describing the tools, equipment and techniques used to manufacture products in factories with those used by local and regional enterprises including cost and impacts, for example clothing made in factories compared with local handmade garments

comparing the design and production of products, services or environments in Australia and a country in Asia, for example comparing the diversity, availability and properties of preferred materials and the design of public shelters and housing in Indonesia and Australia

investigating the properties of fibres and how these are used to create products, for example designing an experiment to test which fabrics are warmest and explaining how those properties influence what they are used for

nodes.label: Material properties determine selection
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify properties of a material and explain how those properties determine whether it is suitable for a specific designed solution
criteria: Identifies at least two properties of a material
Explains how each property makes the material suitable or unsuitable for a specific purpose
nodes.hinge_reason: Material property reasoning in N1 is prerequisite for P01 (determining appropriate materials) and P03 (selecting and justifying material choices) — students who cannot reason from property to suitability will make unjustified material selections throughout production.

width.minimum: Identify at least two properties of a material and explain how each affects whether the material is appropriate for a specific purpose
width.typical: Describe the properties of multiple materials and explain how those properties determine their use in a designed solution — including household sustainability products, textiles, or structural applications; test or compare materials to determine which best matches the design requirements
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians used material science knowledge to select and prepare fibres for different environmental conditions — for example, twining techniques for string and rope suited to wet, dry, freshwater and saltwater applications
Investigate the properties of fibres and design an experiment to test which fabrics are warmest — explaining how measured properties map to real-world use decisions
Compare materials used in household sustainability products (water storage, insulation, solar panels) — explaining which properties make each material appropriate for its role

modes.reason: Students typically identify properties by name without connecting them to selection decisions. Multiple design contexts — each requiring a different set of properties to be matched — build the habit of reasoning from property to suitability rather than describing properties in isolation.

nodes.label: Tools, equipment and production methods affect outcomes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the tools, equipment and techniques used in production affect the quality and characteristics of the designed solution
criteria: Describes how at least one production tool or technique affects the outcome
Identifies at least one trade-off between different production approaches

width.minimum: Describe how at least one tool or production technique affects the quality or characteristics of a designed solution
width.typical: Compare tools, equipment and techniques across different production contexts (factory, local enterprise, handmade); explain how production scale and methods affect cost, quality and design outcomes — including environmental and social impacts
wider: Compare tools, equipment and techniques used in factories with those used by local and regional enterprises — explaining how scale, cost and design intent differ between mass production and local craft production

Compare design and production of products in Australia and a country in Asia (e.g. Indonesia) — exploring how the availability and preferred properties of materials, and the design of public structures like shelters and housing, differ by context

Describe how systems in public places (community exercise environments, water treatment plants, waste management services) are designed to benefit community life — identifying the material and system properties that make each fit for purpose

modes.reason: Students tend to see production tools as neutral — any tool does the job. Comparing production across scales (factory vs handmade) and cultural contexts (Australia vs Asia) makes visible how tool choice and technique are themselves design decisions with trade-offs for quality, cost and cultural fit.

descriptors.title: Investigate needs and processes
descriptors.description: Investigate needs or opportunities for designing, and the materials, components, tools, equipment and processes needed to create designed solutions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore needs or opportunities for designing, and test materials, components, tools, equipment and processes to make designed solutions (AC9TDE4P01). They have explored and tested. They have not yet investigated systematically — the shift is from exploring/testing to purposeful investigation with a view to making design decisions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate needs or opportunities for designing and determine the materials, components, tools, equipment and processes required — including sustainability considerations and comparative evaluation of options.
elaborations: investigating First Nations Australians' traditional fibre sources as potential commercial solutions for biodegradable string or rope, and researching the materials, systems, components, tools and equipment needed

surveying people in the school community about their needs in order to design an appropriate product, service or environment that addresses the need, for example planning the requirements for a community meal, creating more shade in the school by determining where trees could be planted or designing a security system for the community garden

investigating designed solutions from around the world to make suitable, quality decisions that meet needs or opportunities, for example locating information online about small-space gardening ideas from different countries and judging their suitability for the local environment

investigating the importance of complementary parts of working systems by deconstructing the components, structure and purpose of products, services or environments, for example labelling a diagram of a robotic weeder or vacuum cleaner and explaining the function of parts

testing a range of materials, components, tools and equipment to determine the appropriate technologies needed to make products, services or environments, for example the materials for a product such as a rubber-band-powered vehicle or item of protective clothing

investigating how to minimise material use and manage waste by comparing the environmental and social impacts of materials, components, tools and equipment, for example comparing the cost and environmental impact of repurposing an old item of clothing to create a carry bag with buying a new one, or using vegetable scraps to make a healthy soup versus buying takeaway soup

nodes.label: Investigating a need or opportunity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate a need or opportunity for designing by gathering information from multiple sources and identifying what a solution must achieve
criteria: Identifies a need or opportunity with evidence from at least two sources
States what a solution must achieve — not just what is wrong
nodes.hinge_reason: Thin investigation in N1 cascades into every downstream phase — design ideas (P02), material selection (N2, P03), and evaluation criteria (P04) all depend on having accurately characterised what the solution must achieve. An underspecified need produces solutions that solve the wrong problem.

width.minimum: Identify a need or opportunity and investigate it using at least two sources (e.g. surveying users, examining existing solutions, researching online) — summarising what a solution must achieve
width.typical: Survey users in a school or community context to identify a need; investigate existing solutions from around the world to assess suitability; identify the key requirements a designed solution must meet — including functional, social and sustainability requirements
wider: Investigate First Nations Australians' traditional fibre sources as potential commercial solutions for biodegradable string or rope — researching the materials, systems, components and processes needed to develop them commercially
Investigate small-space gardening solutions from different countries and judge their suitability for the local environment — explaining what factors determine suitability

Survey school community members about a specific need (e.g. more shade, a security system for the community garden, a community meal) — documenting needs and constraints that a designed solution must address

modes.reason: Students often investigate a single, self-identified need without testing it against actual users. Multiple investigation contexts — each with different stakeholders and information sources — build the habit of grounding needs in evidence rather than assumption.

nodes.label: Determining required materials, components and processes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can determine what materials, components, tools, equipment and processes are needed to create a designed solution — and compare options
criteria: Identifies at least two options for a material or component
Compares options using at least one criterion and justifies the selection

width.minimum: Identify at least two options for a key material or component and explain which is more appropriate for the design intention, considering at least one sustainability factor
width.typical: Test or research materials, components, tools and equipment to determine which are appropriate for the design; compare options on multiple criteria including function, cost, availability, safety and environmental impact; explain how minimising material use and managing waste affects production decisions
wider: Investigate how to minimise material use and manage waste by comparing the environmental and social impacts of alternative approaches — e.g. repurposing an old item of clothing to create a carry bag versus buying a new one
Deconstruct a product (e.g. a robotic weeder, a vacuum cleaner) to identify its components and explain the function of each — connecting component design to the product's overall purpose
Investigate complementary parts of a working system by identifying how each component's function depends on the others — explaining why changing one component would affect the whole system

modes.reason: Students typically select materials based on familiarity rather than systematic comparison. The reasoning scaffold — identify options → compare on criteria → justify selection — makes material selection a design decision rather than a default choice.

descriptors.title: Iterate and communicate designs
descriptors.description: Generate, iterate and communicate design ideas, decisions and processes using technical terms and graphical representation techniques, including using digital tools
descriptors.knowledge: Students can generate and communicate design ideas and decisions using appropriate attributions, technical terms and graphical representation techniques (AC9TDE4P02). They have generated and communicated ideas. They have not yet iterated — systematically refining designs based on evaluation — or used the full range of representation techniques including scale, symbols, digital mapping and modelling tools.
descriptors.endpoint: Students generate a range of design ideas, iterate and improve them based on evaluation, and communicate decisions and processes using technical terms and graphical representation including digital tools.
elaborations: generating a range of design ideas for products, services or environments using prior knowledge, skills and research, for example a security system for a community garden, a product made from a repurposed item of clothing, a permaculture vegetable patch or a healthy meal for a family picnic

analysing, modifying and developing design ideas to enhance and improve the sustainability of the product, service, environment or system, for example analysing eco-friendly alternatives to non-recyclable decorations for a community event or replacing paper-based newsletters with online formats

representing and communicating design ideas using modelling and drawing standards including the use of digital tools, for example including scale, symbols and codes in plans and diagrams; using pictorial maps and aerial views; and using digital mapping applications or infographics to present research and ideas to others
developing and using models to iterate and improve design ideas, for example using modelling applications to design the layout and features of an enclosure for a chosen animal

experimenting with materials, tools and equipment to refine design decisions and processes, for example considering the selection of materials and joining techniques to suit the purpose of a product, such as a pop-up book, a fabric bag or an electric circuit

considering the social values and ethics of clients when designing an environment, for example interviewing users of a space or seeking permission to use designs or images created by others including respect of cultural and intellectual property

nodes.label: Generating design ideas using prior knowledge and research
nodes.checkpoint: Students can generate a range of design ideas for a product, service or environment drawing on prior knowledge, skills and research
criteria: Generates at least two meaningfully distinct design ideas
Ideas are grounded in at least one source of prior knowledge or research

width.minimum: Generate at least two distinct design ideas for the same need, drawing on prior knowledge and at least one research source
width.typical: Generate a range of design ideas for products, services or environments using prior knowledge, skills and research; represent ideas through sketches, diagrams or models; consider functional, aesthetic and sustainability dimensions across ideas
wider: Generate design ideas for an eco-friendly alternative to a non-recyclable product used in a community event — researching what sustainable alternatives exist before generating original ideas
Generate design ideas for an animal enclosure using modelling applications — iterating the layout and features based on the animal's environmental and behavioural needs

Consider the social values and ethics of clients when designing an environment — interviewing users of a space or seeking permission for designs/images from others, including respect for cultural and intellectual property

modes.reason: Students who only ever design the first thing they think of have a narrow ideation repertoire. Accumulated experience generating ideas across different product, service and environment types — each with different constraints — builds the range students can draw on when a novel design problem is encountered.

nodes.label: Representing design ideas using technical terms and graphical techniques
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent and communicate design ideas using appropriate graphical techniques — including scale, symbols, plans, aerial views and digital tools
criteria: Uses at least one graphical convention (scale, symbols, codes, or aerial view) in a design representation
Uses technical terms to describe at least one design decision
nodes.hinge_reason: A design idea that has not been clearly represented using graphical conventions cannot be systematically analysed or modified in N3 — iteration requires a stable, readable design artifact to work from. Students who cannot represent ideas cannot iterate on them.

width.minimum: Represent at least one design idea using a labelled diagram or plan that includes at least one graphical convention (scale, symbols, or codes)
width.typical: Represent design ideas using a range of techniques — plans with scale and symbols, pictorial maps, aerial views, digital mapping tools or infographics; use appropriate technical terms when describing designs to others; select the representation technique that best communicates the design intent
wider: Use a digital modelling or mapping application to represent a design idea — for example, designing the layout and features of an animal enclosure or a community garden using digital tools
Create an infographic that presents research and design ideas to others — combining visual representation with supporting data and technical terms
Represent a design using pictorial maps and aerial views, explaining why this technique communicates the spatial relationships better than a flat plan

modes.reason: Students default to a single familiar representation technique (e.g. a labelled sketch) regardless of what the design problem needs. Different design contexts that call for different techniques — aerial view for a garden layout, diagram with symbols for a circuit, 3D model for a structure — build representation repertoire.

nodes.label: Iterating designs based on evaluation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse and modify a design idea to improve it — iterating based on sustainability, function or feedback
criteria: Identifies at least one design weakness based on a criterion
Describes a modification that addresses the identified weakness and explains why

width.minimum: Identify at least one weakness or gap in a design idea and describe a modification that addresses it
width.typical: Analyse a design idea against functional, sustainability and aesthetic criteria; modify and develop the design to improve it — documenting what changed and why; use materials, tools or equipment experimentally to refine design decisions before committing to a final approach
wider: Analyse eco-friendly alternatives to non-recyclable decorations for a community event — iterating the design to improve sustainability while maintaining function and aesthetics
Use modelling (physical or digital) to test and iterate a design idea — for example, trialling material joining techniques or component arrangements before making final choices
Replace a paper-based process with a digital equivalent (e.g. newsletters with online formats) — iterating the design to meet the same communication need more sustainably

modes.reason: Iteration integrates the evaluation from node 1 (what are the criteria?) and the representation skills from node 2 (how to document changes?) into a design improvement act. Students who generate and evaluate but don't modify have completed analysis but not design iteration — the modification is the learning.

descriptors.title: Use suitable materials and techniques
descriptors.description: Select and use suitable materials, components, tools, equipment and techniques to safely make designed solutions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can select and use materials, components, tools, equipment and techniques to safely make designed solutions (AC9TDE4P03). They have selected and used tools and materials with guidance. They have not yet matched selection decisions to design intention with explicit justification, or applied the full range of safety, hygiene and environmental considerations across material types.
descriptors.endpoint: Students select materials, components, tools, equipment and techniques that match the design intention and use them safely — applying appropriate safety, hygiene and environmental practices for the context.
elaborations: matching material and joining techniques to the design intention, for example accurately and safely cutting and sewing the fabric pieces to make a community banner or joining components to produce an electric circuit

using appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) required for the use of some tools and equipment, for example protective eyewear and working safely, responsibly and cooperatively to ensure safe work areas, for example the safe use of equipment when making a water-resistant, floating craft

choosing appropriate materials, tools, equipment and techniques for a specific purpose, for example when safely and hygienically preparing food, cultivating garden beds or constructing electronic products

identifying work practices that show an understanding of nutrition, environmental considerations, hygiene and food safety when designing and making a food product, for example washing fruit and vegetables carefully to remove residues, safe disposal of cooking oils to avoid environmental damage, refrigerated storage of highly perishable foods, being aware of food allergies

nodes.label: Matching materials and techniques to the design intention
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select materials and techniques that match the design intention and explain why each choice is appropriate
criteria: Selects materials and techniques appropriate for the design intention
Explains the selection by referencing at least one relevant material property or technique characteristic
nodes.hinge_reason: Material and technique selection in N1 determines what safety practices apply in N2 — students who cannot match materials to design intention will select inappropriate tools or techniques, making N2's safety and hygiene requirements impossible to apply correctly.

width.minimum: Select a material and technique for a specific task and explain why each matches the design intention — referencing at least one material property
width.typical: Choose appropriate materials, tools, equipment and techniques for a specific design purpose; explain how the selection matches the design intention — considering function, aesthetics and sustainability; demonstrate that the selection produces the intended result
wider: Match material and joining techniques to the design intention for a textile project (e.g. a community banner, a fabric bag) — accurately cutting and joining fabric pieces as specified by the design
Select and sequence materials, tools and equipment for an electronic product — explaining how each component choice supports the circuit's intended function
Select and justify materials for a water-resistant, floating craft — explaining which material properties (density, water resistance, structural strength) determine the selection

modes.reason: Students typically select familiar materials by habit rather than matching properties to design intention. Multiple production contexts — textiles, electronics, food, structural — each requiring different property reasoning help students build the habit of justifying selection against design requirements rather than defaulting to familiarity.

nodes.label: Working safely and applying food, hygiene and environmental practices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and apply the relevant safety, hygiene and environmental practices for their production context
criteria: Applies at least two relevant safety or hygiene practices correctly for the production context
Can explain why each practice is required

width.minimum: Identify at least two relevant safety or hygiene practices for a specific production task and apply them correctly
width.typical: Apply appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE), safe work practices, hygiene standards and environmental considerations relevant to the production context — whether food preparation, garden cultivation or construction of electronic or structural products; explain why each practice is required
wider: Apply food safety and hygiene practices in preparing a food product — including washing produce to remove residues, safe disposal of cooking oils, refrigerated storage of perishables, and managing food allergen risks
Apply safe work practices for construction tasks (e.g. protective eyewear, safe tool handling) — explaining how each practice prevents a specific risk
Identify environmental considerations when making with materials — e.g. safe disposal of chemical residues, minimising material waste, selecting materials with lower environmental impact

modes.reason: Safety and hygiene practices require consistent application across contexts, not just recognition. Students who can name practices but don't apply them consistently need deliberate practice opportunities where the habit is formed through repetition across different production contexts.

descriptors.title: Negotiate criteria and evaluate
descriptors.description: Negotiate design criteria including sustainability to evaluate design ideas, processes and solutions
