Reflect on how safe practice decisions affected production efficiency — were any safety measures unnecessarily restrictive or insufficiently protective?

modes.reason: Reflecting on safe practice reinforces the habit of safety awareness — students who review what worked and what didn't build more robust safe practice habits for future projects.

descriptors.title: Develop criteria collaboratively
descriptors.description: develop design criteria collaboratively including sustainability to evaluate design ideas, processes and solutions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can negotiate design criteria, including sustainability, to evaluate design ideas, processes and solutions (AC9TDE6P04). They have used given or negotiated criteria but have not yet developed criteria collaboratively from scratch, incorporated Safety by Design principles, or used evaluation to drive iterative modification of processes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop design criteria collaboratively — covering accessibility, aesthetics, functionality, sustainability and Safety by Design principles — and use these criteria to evaluate design ideas, processes and solutions, iterating and modifying based on evaluation.
elaborations: developing design criteria collaboratively to evaluate designed solutions in terms of accessibility, aesthetics, functionality and sustainability, for example recording design goals from people interviewed as prospective users of the finished product, service or environment or including life cycle assessment criteria
developing design criteria including Safety by Design principles, for example do the ideas promote safety through prevention, protection and proactive change
re-evaluating, iterating and modifying design processes to improve efficiency and increase production, for example when mass producing a product for an enterprise or improving sustainability

evaluating designed solutions and processes and transferring new knowledge and skills to future design projects, for example considering project planning skills learnt in producing an engineered product and using them in future projects

nodes.label: What makes good design criteria
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what design criteria are and why they need to cover multiple dimensions including sustainability
criteria: Identifies at least three dimensions that design criteria should address
Explains why criteria-based evaluation is more useful than personal preference
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who develop vague or single-dimension criteria at Node 2 will produce evaluations at Nodes 3–5 that miss trade-offs between dimensions — the multi-dimensional criteria framework must be understood before it can be applied collaboratively or used to drive iteration.

width.minimum: Identify at least three dimensions that design criteria should address (e.g. accessibility, aesthetics, functionality, sustainability); explain why evaluating against criteria is more useful than evaluating by personal preference
width.typical: Explain how criteria across different dimensions can complement or conflict; identify Safety by Design principles (prevention, protection, proactive change) as a specific criteria framework
wider: Apply life cycle assessment as a criteria framework — how does evaluating across the full product lifecycle change what criteria are prioritised?
Limited width — understanding what criteria are is a single conceptual insight. The breadth comes from applying criteria to different design challenges at later nodes.

modes.reason: Students who develop vague criteria ('make it good') or single-dimension criteria ('make it sustainable') will produce evaluations that miss important trade-offs. Understanding that criteria must be specific, multi-dimensional and assessable is the foundation for useful evaluation at Nodes 2 and 3.

nodes.label: Developing criteria collaboratively
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop design criteria through collaboration, incorporating input from multiple perspectives including potential users
criteria: Develops at least three criteria collaboratively
At least one criterion addresses sustainability
Criteria are specific enough to evaluate a design against
nodes.hinge_reason: The collaboratively developed criteria from this node are the evaluation instrument for Nodes 3, 4 and 5 — without specific, multi-dimensional criteria in hand, students cannot apply them to existing products, drive iterative design decisions, or conduct meaningful final evaluation.

width.minimum: Develop at least three design criteria collaboratively with peers; ensure at least one addresses sustainability
width.typical: Develop criteria collaboratively by recording goals from prospective users, incorporating accessibility and Safety by Design principles, and ensuring criteria are specific enough to evaluate against
wider: Develop criteria through consultation with community members from diverse backgrounds, including those who communicate in languages other than English
Compare criteria developed by different groups for the same design challenge — how does who participates change what gets prioritised?

modes.reason: Developing criteria collaboratively surfaces different perspectives only when students encounter diverse stakeholders and communities. A group of similar students will develop similar criteria. Seeing how criteria change when different community members participate — including those from diverse backgrounds or who communicate in languages other than English — builds understanding that criteria are not neutral.

nodes.label: Applying criteria to analyse existing products
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply collaboratively developed criteria to evaluate existing designed solutions and extract insights that inform their own design brief.
criteria: Evaluates at least one existing product against collaboratively developed criteria
Identifies at least one design insight that will inform their own solution

width.minimum: Evaluate at least one existing product against two collaboratively developed criteria; identify at least one design insight that will inform your own solution.
width.typical: Evaluate multiple existing products against all developed criteria; compare what works and what doesn't; document insights as design constraints or opportunities for your own solution.
wider: Compare existing products from different cultural or geographic contexts against the same criteria — how does context change what 'good design' means?
Evaluate products at different price or quality tiers and explain how criteria satisfaction varies.

modes.reason: Applying criteria to existing products requires students to reason from evidence: criterion → what does the product do → does it satisfy the criterion → what does this tell us about our own design. Students who describe products without applying criteria produce observations rather than insights.

nodes.label: Evaluating and iterating during design
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate design ideas and processes against criteria during the design cycle and iterate based on that evaluation.
criteria: Evaluates a design against at least two criteria during the design process
Modifies the design based on the evaluation and explains the change

width.minimum: Evaluate a design against at least two criteria during the design process; identify at least one improvement and modify the design accordingly.
width.typical: Evaluate and iterate across the design process — not just the final product; re-evaluate after modification to confirm improvement; document what changed and why.
wider: Transfer evaluation skills from one design challenge to another — what criteria and lessons carry across contexts?
Limited width — iterative evaluation is a consistent process. The breadth comes from the variety of design challenges.

modes.reason: Evaluating and iterating during design requires applying collaboratively developed criteria (node 2) to live design decisions. Students who treat evaluation as a final step rather than a design tool produce designs that don't improve through the process.

nodes.label: Final evaluation against criteria
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate a completed designed solution against all collaboratively developed criteria and articulate what they would change in a future iteration.
criteria: Evaluates the completed solution against all collaboratively developed criteria
Identifies at least one specific improvement for a future iteration

width.minimum: Evaluate the completed solution against at least two collaboratively developed criteria; identify at least one thing that would be done differently.
width.typical: Evaluate the completed solution across all criteria dimensions; reflect on how the design process shaped the outcome; identify improvements for a future iteration and explain why.
wider: Evaluate how iterative modification throughout the project improved the final outcome compared to what an initial design would have produced.
Assess how well the collaboratively developed criteria captured what actually mattered — would you develop different criteria next time?

modes.reason: Final evaluation requires students to reason from evidence across the whole project: what did the criteria require → what did the solution achieve → where did it fall short → what would change. Students who produce vague reflections have not applied criteria rigorously.

descriptors.title: Manage time, cost and production
descriptors.description: develop project plans to individually and collaboratively manage time, cost and production of designed solutions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can develop project plans that include consideration of resources to individually and collaboratively make designed solutions (AC9TDE6P05). They have planned with resources in mind but have not yet managed time, cost and production as explicit planning variables, or used planning tools to track and evaluate progress.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop project plans that explicitly manage time, cost and production of designed solutions, including interpreting drawings to identify resources, estimating time for production stages, identifying and minimising risks, and evaluating decisions throughout production.
elaborations: interpreting drawings to plan resources and production steps needed to produce products, services or environments for specific purposes, for example identifying resource requirements from specifications on a labelled drawing and collaboratively developing a detailed procedure

identifying risks and how to minimise them, organising time, evaluating decisions and managing resources to ensure successful project completion, for example using digital tools to keep track of tasks, resources, expenses and deadlines

investigating the time needed for each step of production, for example estimating time allocations on a planning template for the different stages of the design process needed to produce a clock, acoustic speaker or desk lamp using prior knowledge, research and testing

nodes.label: Planning resources and steps from drawings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret design drawings to identify the resources and production steps needed to produce a designed solution
criteria: Identifies materials, tools and steps from a drawing or specification
Lists steps in a logical production sequence
nodes.hinge_reason: Errors in interpreting drawings propagate into every subsequent node — incorrect resource lists at Node 1 produce inaccurate time and cost estimates at Node 2, incomplete risk registers at Node 3, and production steps that cannot be executed at Node 4.

width.minimum: Given a labelled drawing or specification, identify the materials, tools and production steps needed; list them in a logical sequence
width.typical: Interpret drawings to collaboratively develop a detailed procedure; identify resource requirements from specifications including quantities, tools and equipment needed for each step
wider: Limited width — interpreting drawings for production planning is a consistent skill. The breadth comes from the variety of products being planned, not from the interpretation process itself.

modes.reason: Interpreting technical drawings accurately requires practice — students need repeated experience reading specifications, identifying resource requirements and translating drawings into step sequences. Errors in interpretation propagate into production.

nodes.label: Managing time and cost
nodes.checkpoint: Students can estimate time allocations for production stages, track costs, and organise schedules using planning templates or digital tools
criteria: Creates a plan with at least three steps, time estimates and responsibilities
Plan is organised using a template or digital tool
nodes.hinge_reason: Time and cost estimates from this node feed directly into Node 3 risk planning — without realistic time allocations and budget tracking, students cannot identify which stages are at risk of overrun or resource constraint, making the risk register at Node 3 speculative rather than evidence-based.

width.minimum: Create a plan that includes at least three production steps with time estimates and identifies who is responsible for each
width.typical: Use a planning template or digital tool to record tasks, time estimates, critical dates and responsibilities; estimate time allocations using prior knowledge, research and testing; track costs against a budget
wider: Use digital project management tools to track tasks, resources, expenses and deadlines across a complex project
Estimate and compare time allocations for different production stages — then compare estimates against actual time to improve future planning

modes.reason: Time and cost management applies differently across different production types — textile projects, food production, engineering systems each have different time profiles and cost structures. Students who only plan for one production type develop planning habits that do not transfer. Seeing how time and cost variables behave across different production contexts builds transferable planning skill.

nodes.label: Identifying project risks and contingencies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify project-level risks — time overruns, resource constraints, scope changes — and plan contingency strategies before production begins.
criteria: Identifies at least two project-level risks before production begins
Plans a contingency strategy for each identified risk
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a risk register and contingency plan, Node 4 (managing risks during production) has nothing to apply — students who have not anticipated risks before production cannot respond systematically when they arise.

width.minimum: Identify at least two project-level risks (e.g. running out of time, materials unavailable); plan a contingency strategy for each.
width.typical: Identify and plan contingencies for risks across the project — time, resources, dependencies, scope; document strategies and trigger conditions for each contingency.
wider: Develop contingency plans for when production steps take longer than estimated — what can be adjusted without compromising the design?
Assess long-term health and environmental impacts of production choices, not just immediate safety risks.

modes.reason: Risk identification requires prospective reasoning: identify what could go wrong → assess likelihood and severity → determine mitigation strategy → decide when to trigger contingency. Students who list risks without this reasoning chain produce registers they cannot act on.

nodes.label: Managing risks during production
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply planned risk mitigation strategies during production and respond to unexpected hazards as they arise.
criteria: Applies at least one planned mitigation strategy during production
Responds appropriately to at least one hazard that arises

width.minimum: Apply at least one planned mitigation strategy during production; identify and respond to at least one unexpected hazard.
width.typical: Apply risk mitigation strategies consistently throughout production; manage workspace hazards as they arise; document any unexpected risks encountered.
wider: Compare how planned vs actual risks differed — what hazards emerged that weren't anticipated?
Evaluate whether planned mitigation strategies were effective or needed adjustment during production.

modes.reason: Managing risks during production requires consistent application of safe practices — PPE, workspace management, equipment handling. Repeated practice across production tasks builds the automatic habit.

nodes.label: Evaluating decisions during production
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate production decisions at key points during making and adjust the plan when circumstances change.
criteria: Evaluates at least one production decision during the project
Explains what changed and why the adjustment was needed

width.minimum: Evaluate at least one production decision during the project — explain what changed and why the adjustment was needed.
width.typical: Evaluate decisions at key points rather than only at the end; adjust the plan when production takes longer than estimated or when resources change; document each adjustment.
wider: Develop contingency plans for when production steps take longer than estimated — what can be adjusted without compromising the design?
Compare how different adjustment decisions affected the final outcome.

modes.reason: Evaluating during production integrates risk identification (node 3) and time/cost management (node 2) — students must apply both to make and justify adjustments as production unfolds.

nodes.label: Reflecting on production after completion
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on how production decisions held up against the plan and identify what they would do differently in a future project.
criteria: Reflects on at least one production decision after completion
Identifies a specific improvement for a future project with justification

width.minimum: Reflect on at least one production decision after completion — did it hold up, and what would you change?
width.typical: Reflect on how planning decisions (time estimates, risk mitigation, resource choices) affected the final outcome; identify specific improvements for a future production project.
wider: Compare time and cost estimates against actuals — use the comparison to produce improved estimates for a similar future project.
Evaluate how contingency decisions affected the final design quality — what trade-offs were made and were they worth it?

modes.reason: Post-completion reflection requires students to reason backwards from outcome to decision: what was the outcome → what decision produced it → was that the right call → what would change. Students who produce generic reflections ('it went well') have not applied this reasoning.

descriptors.title: Ethics, security and sustainability in DT occupations
descriptors.description: analyse how people in design and technologies occupations consider ethical, security and sustainable factors to innovate and improve products, services and environments
descriptors.knowledge: Students can analyse how people in design and technologies occupations consider ethical and sustainability factors when designing solutions (AC9TDE8K01). They can identify how designers respond to community needs and sustainability constraints. They have not yet analysed how ethical, security and sustainability factors combine to drive innovation, nor examined product life cycle thinking, mass production systems, or the role of global professional collaboration.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse how people in design and technologies occupations integrate ethical, security and sustainability considerations — including product life cycle thinking, mass production ethics, and professional collaboration — to innovate and improve products, services and environments.
elaborations: examining sustainability factors influencing the design and production of a solution developed by First Nations Australians, such as the sustainable production of culturally significant pigments
analysing design and technologies professions and their contributions to society, for example engineers working in disaster recovery or empowering communities
recognising the impact of past designed solutions when creating solutions for preferred futures
considering the factors that influence design and manufacture and the work of professional designers including time, access to skills, knowledge, finance, expertise in global engineering
explaining how product life cycle thinking can influence decision-making related to design and technologies
examining mass production systems taking into account ethics and sustainability considerations
explaining the consequences of ethical and sustainability decisions for products, services and environments

nodes.label: Product life cycle thinking
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what product life cycle thinking is and how it influences design decisions.
criteria: Correctly explains what product life cycle thinking considers beyond the point of sale
Gives a specific example of how it has influenced at least one design decision
nodes.hinge_reason: Life cycle thinking is the analytical framework used at N2, N3 and N4 — students who cannot apply it cannot evaluate mass production systems, professional design contributions, or the consequences of decisions through a sustainability lens.

width.minimum: Explain what product life cycle thinking means and give one example of how it has influenced a design decision (e.g. material choice, design for disassembly, re-use planning).
width.typical: Explain how life cycle thinking shifts decisions across the design process — material selection, production method, packaging, end-of-life — and give examples of products where life cycle thinking has produced a different design outcome than conventional approaches.
wider: Analyse the full product life cycle of a specific everyday object and identify where the greatest environmental impact occurs — explain what design change at that stage would have most effect
Compare a product designed with life cycle thinking (e.g. modular, repairable) with a conventional equivalent — evaluate the trade-offs for manufacturer, consumer and environment

Investigate how First Nations Australians' traditional production practices embody life cycle thinking — for example, the sustainable production and use of culturally significant pigments through calcination

modes.reason: Life cycle thinking is abstract without concrete examples. Multiple product cases — designed for disassembly, with lower-carbon material substitutions, and traditional sustainable practices — each make a different aspect of the concept visible. Students who see only one case often reduce it to recycling.

nodes.label: Ethics and sustainability in mass production
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse ethics and sustainability considerations in mass production systems, including why manufacturers make different versions of the same product.
criteria: Identifies at least one ethical and one sustainability consideration in a specific mass production context
Explains how each consideration affects a production or design decision

width.minimum: Identify at least one ethical and one sustainability consideration in a mass production system; explain how each affects design or production decisions.
width.typical: Analyse a mass production system (e.g. food, clothing, electronics) — identify ethical considerations (labour, supply chain, intellectual property) and sustainability considerations (materials, waste, energy); explain why producers create different product versions and how product life cycle strategies affect these decisions.
wider: Examine the mass production of a food, clothing or footwear product — analyse the ethical and sustainability trade-offs at each stage of the production chain
Investigate what complete product life cycle strategies look like for a high-volume product and evaluate how realistic these are at scale
Compare how a multinational manufacturer and a small local producer of the same product type approach ethics and sustainability differently — explain the structural reasons for the differences

nodes.label: Professional roles and global collaboration
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how design and technologies professionals contribute to society and collaborate across global contexts.
criteria: Names a specific profession and connects it to a concrete societal contribution
Identifies at least one constraint (time, cost, expertise, geography) that shapes professional practice

width.minimum: Describe one design or technologies profession and explain how it contributes to society through at least one example project or outcome.
width.typical: Analyse the contributions of design and technologies professions — engineers, designers, technologists — to addressing societal needs; explain how factors such as time, finance, expertise and global manufacturing partnerships influence professional practice; examine at least one example of international collaboration.
wider: Analyse the collaboration between Australian and Vietnamese engineers on the Cao Lanh Bridge — identify what each party contributed and what made the collaboration necessary
Investigate how engineers working in disaster recovery or community energy access navigate ethical, sustainability and resource constraints simultaneously
Examine how rapid prototyping manufacturers in global supply chains change the relationship between Australian designers and production — evaluate the benefits and risks

modes.reason: Professional contributions are best understood through contrasting cases — local vs international, engineering vs design vs technology, disaster recovery vs commercial product development. Multiple contexts prevent students reducing 'contribution to society' to a single profession type.

nodes.label: Consequences of ethical and sustainability decisions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse the consequences of ethical and sustainability decisions for products, services and environments, including the accessibility of public environments and infrastructure.
criteria: Identifies a specific ethical or sustainability decision and names at least one concrete consequence
Explains the mechanism connecting the decision to the consequence (not just stating both)

width.minimum: Describe one consequence — intended or unintended — of an ethical or sustainability design decision for a product, service or environment.
width.typical: Analyse how ethical and sustainability decisions in design produce consequences across users, environments and communities — including cases where decisions benefit some users while disadvantaging others; consider accessibility, safety, environmental impact and community outcomes.
wider: Analyse the design of a public environment (e.g. managed public space, road corridor) for its accessibility, sustainability and safety — evaluate how competing design goals were balanced
Examine the design of infrastructure to reduce fire risk in rural communities — identify what ethical, sustainability and safety decisions shaped the design and what the consequences were
Investigate an instance where a design decision improved sustainability but reduced accessibility or vice versa — evaluate how the trade-off should have been managed

modes.reason: Consequence analysis requires students to reason forward from decision to outcome to affected party — without this scaffold, students describe what was decided rather than analyse what followed. The reasoning chain (decision → mechanism → consequence → who is affected and how) is the key skill.

descriptors.title: Innovation, enterprise and emerging technologies
descriptors.description: analyse the impact of innovation, enterprise and emerging technologies on designed solutions for global preferred futures
descriptors.knowledge: Students can analyse the impact of innovation and the development of technologies on designed solutions and sustainability (AC9TDE8K02). They can identify how innovation responds to community needs. They have not yet examined enterprise responses to technological change, used forecasting or backcasting techniques, or analysed innovation for global preferred futures.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse how innovation, enterprise and emerging technologies interact to create designed solutions — and use forecasting and backcasting techniques to evaluate possible futures and their implications for society.
elaborations: investigating how the knowledges of First Nations Australians have led to the discovery of potential innovative solutions, for example biodegradable polymers using spinifex grass
exploring the ways commercial enterprises respond to the challenges and opportunities of technological change, for example e-commerce, and considering their carbon footprint
investigating scenarios of how the future may unfold and what opportunities and impacts there may be for society using forecasting and backcasting techniques
examining real-world problems and understanding basic needs when considering designed solutions, for example students collaborating to design solutions to challenges in the Asia region

nodes.label: How enterprise responds to technological change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how commercial enterprises respond to the challenges and opportunities of technological change.
criteria: Identifies a specific technological change and describes how an enterprise responded
Explains what drove the response (market opportunity, competitive pressure, regulation, etc.)
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who don't understand how enterprises respond to technological change cannot productively apply forecasting and backcasting at N2 — the scenarios have no grounding in how real design and enterprise decisions are made.

width.minimum: Describe one way a commercial enterprise has responded to a technological change — either adapting an existing model or creating a new one; explain what drove the response.
width.typical: Analyse how commercial enterprises respond to technological change — including changes to business models (e.g. e-commerce), carbon footprint considerations, and the competitive dynamics that drive innovation; examine at least two examples across different sectors.
wider: Compare how two enterprises in the same sector responded differently to the same technological shift — analyse why their responses differed and which was more effective
Investigate the carbon footprint implications of e-commerce compared with traditional retail — evaluate whether the convenience benefit is offset by the environmental cost
Examine how a First Nations enterprise has used emerging technology to scale, protect or commercialise traditional knowledge — for example, biodegradable polymers using spinifex grass

modes.reason: Enterprise response patterns need to accumulate across examples before students can reason about them — a single case study doesn't provide the range needed to apply enterprise thinking to novel futures. Multiple enterprise contexts build the schema that forecasting and backcasting can then work with.

nodes.label: Forecasting and backcasting for preferred futures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use forecasting and backcasting techniques to investigate possible futures and evaluate what opportunities and impacts they present.
criteria: Correctly distinguishes forecasting from backcasting
Applies at least one technique to a scenario and identifies at least one implication for society

width.minimum: Describe what forecasting and backcasting are; apply one technique to a scenario and describe one future implication.
width.typical: Apply forecasting (projecting current trends forward) and backcasting (starting from a preferred future and working backward) to a real-world challenge; identify opportunities and impacts for society and particular groups; explain what design or innovation decisions would be needed to move toward the preferred future.
wider: Apply backcasting to a specific global challenge (e.g. food security, clean energy access) — identify the design and technology decisions required at each stage to reach the preferred future
Investigate how the Asia region collaboration scenarios for designed solutions (e.g. collaborative design for pandemic response) used future-oriented thinking to define the problem
Compare forecasting and backcasting outputs for the same scenario — analyse what each technique reveals that the other doesn't

modes.reason: Forecasting and backcasting are reasoning techniques — students who don't apply a structured process produce vague futures rather than analysed scenarios. The scaffold (identify trend / preferred state → project or trace back → identify implications → identify design decisions) makes the technique productive.

nodes.label: Innovation from diverse knowledge systems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how diverse knowledge systems — including First Nations knowledge — have led to innovative designed solutions.
criteria: Identifies a specific innovation and the knowledge system it drew on
Explains what aspect of that knowledge system enabled the innovation

width.minimum: Describe one example of innovation that drew on a non-Western or First Nations knowledge system; explain what knowledge was applied and what problem it addressed.
width.typical: Analyse how diverse knowledge systems have contributed to designed solutions — including First Nations Australian knowledges (e.g. spinifex biodegradable polymers), traditional ecological knowledge applied to contemporary materials, and cross-cultural design collaborations; evaluate how these contributions challenge assumptions about where innovation originates.
wider: Research how spinifex grass polymers are being developed as a sustainable material — analyse what First Nations knowledge was the foundation and what contemporary technology extended it

Investigate a real-world challenge in the Asia region where collaboration across knowledge systems produced a designed solution that a single knowledge system could not — explain what each system contributed
Examine how intellectual property frameworks interact with First Nations knowledge in design contexts — what protections exist and where gaps remain

modes.reason: Students often treat innovation as originating solely from Western science and technology. Diverse knowledge system examples — First Nations materials science, traditional ecological engineering, cross-cultural design — each challenge this assumption from a different angle and are better understood together than individually.

descriptors.title: Materials, force, motion and energy in engineered systems
descriptors.description: analyse and make judgements on how the characteristics and properties of materials are combined with force, motion and energy to control engineered systems
descriptors.knowledge: Students can analyse how force, motion and energy are used to manipulate and control engineered systems (AC9TDE8K03). They can identify material properties in functional contexts. They have not yet made judgements on combinations of material properties with force, motion and energy, nor calculated structural loads or critiqued system effectiveness.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse and make judgements on how material characteristics and properties combine with force, motion and energy to control engineered systems — including calculating forces and loads, and critiquing system effectiveness.
elaborations: investigating the engineering innovations of First Nations Australians, such as spearthrowers and bow and arrow, and how characteristics and properties of materials are used
explaining the way common machines or engineered systems interact and combine properties of materials, force, motion and energy efficiently
calculating forces, reactions and loads in structures and analysing the relationship between materials of properties, forces and safety in engineered systems such as bridges
critiquing the effectiveness of the combinations of materials, forces, energy and motion in an engineered system such as a 3D printer
investigating how the placement of wind turbines in a wind farm affects their performance
investigating the main types of chargers for electric vehicles and their capabilities

nodes.label: Material properties in engineered system design
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how specific material characteristics and properties are selected to perform roles in engineered systems.
criteria: Correctly names at least two material properties and connects each to a specific functional role
Explains why the combination of properties is needed — not just listing each separately
nodes.hinge_reason: Material property identification at N1 is prerequisite for N2 — analysing how force, motion and energy interact with materials requires correctly knowing which properties are relevant. Misidentified properties produce incorrect system analysis.

width.minimum: Identify at least two material properties (e.g. rigidity, flexibility, hardness, tensile strength) and explain why each is needed for a specific function in an engineered system.
width.typical: Analyse how a range of material properties — rigidity, flexibility, hardness, tensile/compressive strength, weight — are combined in a specific engineered system to meet functional requirements; explain why no single material property is sufficient and how combinations address competing demands.
wider: Investigate the engineering of First Nations Australian tools such as spearthrowers — analyse how material properties (rigidity, flexibility, hardness) are exploited in their design and explain the biomechanical advantage achieved

Compare how the same functional requirement (e.g. lightweight strength) is met differently in aerospace, civil engineering and sports equipment — explain what different constraints drive different material selections

modes.reason: Material property recognition needs to be built across multiple material-system pairs before students can reliably select relevant properties for a novel engineered system. Accumulation across contexts (structural, mechanical, thermal) builds the property recognition schema.

nodes.label: Force, motion and energy interactions in systems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how force, motion and energy interact in a specific engineered system, identifying how each component contributes to system control.
criteria: Identifies at least two components in a system and explains how each contributes to system function
Explains how force, motion and energy interact — not just lists components
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot explain how force, motion and energy interact in a system cannot calculate forces correctly at N3 (they don't know what they're calculating) or critique system effectiveness at N4 (they cannot reason about what makes the combination efficient or not).

width.minimum: Describe how force, motion and energy interact in one engineered system (e.g. a crane, a car safety system, a 3D printer); explain the function of at least two components.
width.typical: Analyse how a complex engineered system combines force, motion and energy — explaining the function of multiple components, how they interact, and how the system achieves its purpose efficiently; examine at least one system with safety-critical requirements (e.g. vehicle safety features).
wider: Analyse the force, motion and energy interactions in vehicle safety features (seatbelts, airbags, crumple zones) — explain how each feature controls force transfer to the occupant and why the combination is more effective than any single feature
Investigate how wind turbine placement in a wind farm affects performance — explain the force and energy relationships that determine optimal layout within a given space

modes.reason: Force, motion and energy interactions are best understood through contrasting system types. Safety-critical systems (crumple zones), energy harvesting (wind turbines) and mechanical production (3D printers) each foreground different aspects of the interaction and together build a more complete analytical framework.

nodes.label: Calculating forces and making structural judgements
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate forces, reactions and loads in structures and make judgements about the relationship between material properties, forces and safety.
criteria: Correctly calculates at least one force, reaction or load with appropriate units
Uses the calculation to make a judgement about material requirements or structural safety
nodes.hinge_reason: Force calculation errors at N3 directly produce incorrect structural judgements at N4 — a student who calculates a load incorrectly will judge an adequate structure as inadequate or vice versa.

width.minimum: Calculate at least one force, reaction or load in a simple structure; explain what the calculation tells you about safety or material requirements.
width.typical: Calculate forces, reactions and loads in a structure (e.g. a simple bridge or truss); analyse the relationship between material properties, applied forces and safety margins; make judgements about whether a design is fit for purpose given the calculated loads.
wider: Calculate forces in a bridge structure under load and make a judgement about whether a proposed material meets the safety requirements — explain what would happen if the material were substituted
Investigate how the placement and sizing of structural elements is optimised in a real engineered structure — explain how engineers balance material cost, safety factor and structural performance
Investigate how EV charger selection involves calculating electrical load requirements against vehicle specifications — apply quantitative reasoning to make a recommendation

modes.reason: Force calculation requires procedural accuracy — sign conventions, free body diagrams, reaction forces. Students need sufficient practice with calculation procedures before they can apply them to make analytical judgements. Errors in calculation cascade into incorrect safety conclusions.

nodes.label: Critiquing system effectiveness
nodes.checkpoint: Students can critique the effectiveness of how materials, forces, energy and motion are combined in an engineered system.
criteria: Makes a specific critique — not just description — of how materials, force, motion or energy are combined
Supports the critique with reasoning connected to the system's purpose or safety requirements

width.minimum: Identify at least one strength and one limitation in how an engineered system combines materials, forces and energy; explain what each reveals about the design.
width.typical: Critique an engineered system's effectiveness — analyse how well the combination of materials, force, motion and energy achieves the system's purpose; identify design trade-offs, inefficiencies or safety considerations; make a judgement about whether the system is well-optimised for its purpose.
wider: Critique the effectiveness of a 3D printer as an engineered system — analyse the relationships between its material handling, motion control and energy use and identify where design trade-offs have been made
Evaluate a wind farm layout for efficiency — analyse how turbine placement, force interactions and energy capture are optimised and where further improvement would be possible
Compare two engineered solutions to the same problem (e.g. two bridge designs) and judge which more effectively combines material properties, force management and energy efficiency

modes.reason: Critique requires a judgment framework — students who are asked to evaluate without structure produce descriptive summaries. The reasoning scaffold (what is the system trying to achieve? → how well does each component contribute? → what are the trade-offs? → overall judgement) produces analytical critique.

descriptors.title: Ethical and sustainable food and fibre enterprises
descriptors.description: analyse and make judgements on the ethical, secure and sustainable production and marketing of food and fibre enterprises
descriptors.knowledge: Students can analyse how food and fibre are produced in managed environments and how food and fibre production systems are affected by innovation and sustainability requirements (AC9TDE8K04). They can identify production methods and sustainability considerations. They have not yet made judgements on ethics and security in production and marketing, nor analysed food and water security, digital production tools, or marketing chain impacts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse and make judgements on the ethical, secure and sustainable production and marketing of food and fibre enterprises — including production technology choices, environmental interdependencies, food security, and the marketing chain.
elaborations: analysing grain sources used by First Nations Australians, such as acacia, for their nutrient content and suitability as a sustainable food source
examining emerging production technologies and methods in terms of productivity, profitability and sustainability, including animal welfare considerations
investigating how digital tools could be used to enhance food production systems
investigating the interdependence of plants and animals and comparing the environmental impacts of intensive and extensive production systems
considering the meaning of food and water security and how they may influence design decisions
examining the marketing chain of a range of agricultural products and outlining the effect of product processing and advertising on demand and price

nodes.label: Emerging production technologies and methods
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse emerging production technologies in terms of productivity, profitability and sustainability, including their ethical implications.
criteria: Identifies a specific production technology and correctly assesses at least one sustainability or ethical consideration
Goes beyond description — makes a comparative or evaluative judgement about the technology's implications

width.minimum: Describe one emerging production technology or method (e.g. protected cropping, hydroponics, aquaculture) and identify one productivity benefit and one sustainability or ethical consideration.
width.typical: Analyse emerging production technologies and methods — protected cropping, hydroponics, aquaculture, precision livestock systems — evaluating productivity, profitability and sustainability for each; include animal welfare considerations where relevant; explain how different production systems involve different trade-offs.
wider: Analyse grain sources used by First Nations Australians (e.g. acacia) for their nutrient content and suitability as sustainable food sources in drought-prone regions — compare with conventional cereal crops for productivity and sustainability

Investigate precision agriculture tools (GPS tracking, crop sensors, automated feeding, drones for weed management) and evaluate how digital technologies change the ethics and sustainability profile of production systems
Compare intensive and extensive production systems for a specific animal product — evaluate environmental impact, animal welfare and productivity trade-offs

modes.reason: Production technology trade-offs look different across production types — crop-based systems have different ethical and sustainability tensions than livestock systems, and digital tools introduce different considerations again. Multiple contexts build a more complete analytical picture than a single production type.

nodes.label: Environmental interdependencies in production
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse the interdependence of plants and animals in food and fibre systems and compare the environmental impacts of different production approaches.
criteria: Identifies a specific environmental interdependency in a food or fibre system
Analyses how a production decision affects the interdependency — not just states both separately

width.minimum: Describe one example of environmental interdependence in a food or fibre production system; explain how a production decision affects that interdependence.
width.typical: Analyse the interdependence of plants and animals in production systems — including the impact of pesticide use on non-target species (e.g. bees), comparison of caged vs free-range production, and how production choices cascade through ecosystems; make a judgement about the most sustainable approach given the trade-offs.
wider: Investigate the impact of pesticide use on bee populations in a specific agricultural context — evaluate how the production benefit compares to the ecosystem cost and what alternatives exist
Analyse how food and water security concerns — including water-efficient irrigation and protected cropping — shape production decisions for preferred futures
Compare two production systems for the same product that differ in their environmental footprint — judge which is more sustainable and under what conditions the other approach might be justified

nodes.label: Marketing chains and ethical trade
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine the marketing chain of agricultural products and analyse the effect of processing, advertising and cash crop dynamics on price, demand and communities.
criteria: Identifies at least two distinct stages in a marketing chain
Explains how a decision at one stage affects price, demand or community outcomes at another

width.minimum: Describe at least two stages in the marketing chain of an agricultural product; explain how processing or marketing at one stage affects price or demand.
width.typical: Analyse the marketing chain of a range of agricultural products — from production through processing, distribution and retail to consumer; explain how product processing and advertising affect demand and price; examine the impact of cash crops on communities, including who benefits and who bears risk.
wider: Trace the full marketing chain of a specific agricultural product (e.g. coffee, cotton, cacao) and make a judgement on where ethical trade practices are and aren't present
Examine how food labelling (including country of origin, fair trade, organic) affects consumer decisions and producer pricing — evaluate how effective labelling is as an ethical tool
Investigate the impact of a cash crop economy on a specific community — analyse how dependence on a single export crop affects food security and economic resilience

modes.reason: Marketing chain analysis requires students to trace value and decision-making across multiple actors — producers, processors, distributors, retailers, consumers. Without a structured chain-tracing approach, students focus on production and ignore downstream dynamics that determine who benefits and who bears risk.

descriptors.title: Sensory and functional food properties for healthy eating
descriptors.description: analyse and make judgements on how the sensory and functional properties of food influence the design and preparation of sustainable food solutions for healthy eating
descriptors.knowledge: Students can analyse how the properties of foods determine their preparation and presentation techniques, and how health, food safety and sustainability affect food choices (AC9TDE8K05). They can identify sensory and nutritional properties of food. They have not yet made judgements on how these properties interact in designing sustainable food solutions, nor examined food preservation, trend-driven food innovation, or emerging food technologies.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse and make judgements on how sensory and functional food properties influence the design and preparation of sustainable food solutions for healthy eating — including food preservation, trends, and emerging technologies.
elaborations: analysing how First Nations Australians have long understood techniques to turn plant products into food sources with high nutritional value
experimenting with food preservation methods such as freezing and dehydrating to determine changes to food structure
conducting sensory and nutritional assessment testing of a range of foods to determine how these characteristics might be used to enhance food solutions
determining how the causes of food spoilage can be addressed when preparing, cooking, presenting and storing food items
reflecting on food trends and how they may influence choosing food or designing food solutions for healthy eating
investigating ways innovations may influence human health and sustainability, for example 3D printing of foods, Internet of Things (IoT) in the food supply chain
considering factors that influence the preparation and presentation of foods using a range of techniques to ensure optimum nutrient content, flavour, texture and visual appeal

nodes.label: Sensory and nutritional assessment of food
nodes.checkpoint: Students can conduct or interpret sensory and nutritional assessments of foods and explain how these characteristics inform food solution design.
criteria: Identifies at least two sensory characteristics and explains how each affects food quality or acceptability
Connects assessment findings to a design decision — not just describes the food
nodes.hinge_reason: Sensory and nutritional assessment skills established at N1 are applied at N3 when evaluating food trends — students who cannot conduct or interpret assessments cannot judge whether innovations improve nutritional value or sensory quality.

width.minimum: Describe at least two sensory characteristics (e.g. texture, flavour, colour, aroma) and explain how they influence a food design decision.
width.typical: Conduct or interpret sensory and nutritional assessments across a range of foods; explain how sensory characteristics (flavour, texture, colour, aroma) and nutritional properties interact; use assessment findings to inform decisions about food solution design.
wider: Compare freshly squeezed juice with commercial alternatives through sensory and nutritional assessment — make a judgement on which better serves a healthy eating solution and explain the trade-offs
Analyse how First Nations Australians' understanding of detoxification processes (e.g. cycad nuts) reflects sophisticated knowledge of the functional properties of food
Compare locally grown with imported produce through sensory assessment — evaluate how freshness, seasonality and food miles interact in sustainable food solution design

modes.reason: Sensory assessment requires precision and consistent application of criteria — colour, texture, flavour and aroma each need to be identified and described reliably. Sufficient practice with varied foods builds the assessment fluency that N3 evaluation requires.

nodes.label: Food preservation and spoilage
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how food spoilage occurs and how preservation methods affect food structure, sensory properties and nutritional value.
criteria: Correctly identifies at least one spoilage mechanism and the preservation method that addresses it
Explains how the preservation method changes at least one food property (sensory or nutritional)
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify spoilage causes and preservation responses cannot design food solutions at N3 that are both safe and aligned with food trends — the food safety requirement runs through all food solution design.

width.minimum: Describe one cause of food spoilage and one preservation method; explain how the preservation method changes the food's properties.
width.typical: Explain how different causes of food spoilage (microbial, enzymatic, oxidative) are addressed by different preservation methods; analyse how methods such as freezing, dehydrating, or heat treatment affect food structure, sensory properties and nutritional value; apply safe food handling and storage principles including danger-zone temperatures.
wider: Experiment with dehydration and compare the sensory and nutritional properties of the fresh and dehydrated product — make a judgement on when dehydration is a suitable preservation method

Evaluate multiple preservation methods for the same food against criteria of safety, nutritional retention, sensory quality and sustainability — make a judgement on the best approach for a specific food solution context
Develop a comprehensive food safety checklist for a food service context — explain how each element addresses a specific spoilage or contamination risk

modes.reason: Food safety knowledge requires precision — danger-zone temperatures, contamination vectors, storage requirements. Students need sufficient practice applying these accurately before they can make judgements about preservation method trade-offs. Errors in food safety knowledge have real consequences.

nodes.label: Food trends and sustainable healthy eating
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse food trends and evaluate how they influence food solution design for healthy eating and sustainability.
criteria: Identifies a specific food trend and connects it to both healthy eating and sustainability considerations
Makes a judgement — not just a description — about the trend's merits and limitations

width.minimum: Identify one current food trend and explain how it might influence the design of a food solution for healthy eating.
width.typical: Analyse multiple food trends (e.g. plant-based foods, organic ingredients, insect protein, non-dairy milk, food delivery) and evaluate how each influences food solution design — considering health, sustainability and practicality; make a judgement on which trends genuinely advance healthy and sustainable eating.
wider: Evaluate the health and sustainability claims of two competing food trends (e.g. plant-based meat vs conventional protein, non-dairy milk vs dairy) — make a judgement grounded in nutritional and environmental evidence

Investigate how innovations in food technology (e.g. 3D food printing, IoT food supply chain, AR food labelling) may influence future food solution design — evaluate the potential benefits and risks for healthy eating

Design a healthy canteen item that incorporates a current food trend — document how sensory, nutritional and sustainability considerations shaped the design and use food photography and digital promotion tools

modes.reason: Food trends vary enormously in their health and sustainability basis — some are well-evidenced, others are marketing-driven. Students who evaluate only one trend cannot develop the analytical framework for distinguishing trend from evidence. Multiple contrasting trends — each with different health and sustainability profiles — build this judgement capacity.

descriptors.title: Materials, systems, components, tools and equipment in designed solutions
descriptors.description: analyse and make judgements on how characteristics and properties of materials, systems, components, tools and equipment can be combined to create designed solutions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can analyse how characteristics and properties of materials, systems, components, tools and equipment can be combined to create designed solutions (AC9TDE8K06). They can identify material properties and justify selection decisions. They have not yet made judgements on combinations, nor critiqued environmental consequences of material selection, nor investigated emerging and innovative materials at this level.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse and make judgements on how characteristics and properties of materials, systems, components, tools and equipment can be combined in designed solutions — including environmental consequences of material selection, emerging materials, and justified selection from a broad technology range.
elaborations: analysing how First Nations Australians identified the superior thermal properties of possum fur in developing products such as cloaks including making judgements on how these fibres are sourced
critiquing the design of an existing product to identify environmental consequences of material selection and investigating emerging materials such as bioplastics or seaweed
justifying decisions when selecting from a broad range of technologies — tools, equipment, processes, materials, systems and components
analysing and explaining the ways in which the properties and characteristics of materials have been considered in the design of a product with specific requirements
investigating emerging materials and their impact on design decisions, for example bioplastic material made from discarded potato peels
investigating fibre-based medical textile products and structures used in a medical environment
investigating soft robotics including nanomaterials which enable them to function like human muscles

nodes.label: Environmental consequences of material selection
nodes.checkpoint: Students can critique designed solutions to identify the environmental consequences of material selection and compare with sustainable alternatives.
criteria: Identifies at least one environmental consequence of a specific material selection
Evaluates an alternative material against the original — not just describes it
nodes.hinge_reason: Critiquing environmental consequences of material selection at N1 directly informs N2 judgements about emerging materials — students who haven't developed this evaluative lens cannot make defensible sustainability judgements about new materials.

width.minimum: Identify one environmental consequence of a material used in an existing product; describe one alternative material that would reduce that consequence.
width.typical: Critique an existing product's material selection for environmental consequences — considering carbon footprint, toxicity, biodegradability, and end-of-life options; research at least one emerging or sustainable alternative and evaluate the trade-offs of switching.
wider: Critique the design of common plastic bags and research innovative sustainable alternatives (bioplastics, seaweed-based materials) — make a judgement on which alternative best balances performance, cost and environmental benefit

Analyse how First Nations Australians' use of possum fur (thermal properties, biodegradability, source management) represents sophisticated material knowledge — examine how this is being applied in contemporary high-performance thermal clothing

Investigate how locally sourced materials (e.g. bamboo cross-laminated timber) compare to conventional equivalents on carbon footprint, performance and cost — justify a selection decision for a specific application

modes.reason: Environmental consequences of material selection are highly context-dependent — plastics, textiles, structural materials and fibres each have different environmental profiles and different alternative options. Multiple material contexts build analytical flexibility rather than a single-material conclusion.

nodes.label: Emerging and innovative materials
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate emerging materials and make judgements on their impact on design decisions.
criteria: Describes a specific emerging material's relevant properties
Makes a judgement about how it changes design decisions compared to a conventional alternative

width.minimum: Describe one emerging material and explain how it changes at least one design decision compared to a conventional material.
width.typical: Investigate multiple emerging materials (e.g. bioplastics from waste, soft robotics nanomaterials, fibre-based medical textiles) across different application domains; make judgements about how each changes design possibilities, constraints and sustainability trade-offs.
wider: Investigate bioplastic material made from discarded potato peels — evaluate its properties, applications (buttons, eyeglasses) and limitations compared to conventional plastics

Examine fibre-based medical textiles (e.g. collagen fibre sutures with silk-like strength and biodegradability) — analyse how the combination of properties creates a design solution conventional materials cannot achieve
Investigate soft robotics nanomaterials that enable robot components to function like human muscles — evaluate what design possibilities this opens and what engineering challenges remain

modes.reason: Emerging material judgements develop best across multiple material types — bioplastics, nanomaterials, medical textiles and renewable composites each illuminate different aspects of what makes a material viable for design. A single emerging material provides insufficient range for the 'make judgements' command term.

nodes.label: Justifying selection from a broad technology range
nodes.checkpoint: Students can justify the selection of specific materials, tools, equipment, processes and systems from a broad range of technology options for a design context.
criteria: Selection is justified with reference to specific design requirements — not just preferences
At least one trade-off is acknowledged — why the chosen option is better than at least one alternative for this context
nodes.hinge_reason: The descriptor's command term is 'analyse and make judgements' — students who cannot justify technology selection with structured reasoning against design requirements produce descriptions rather than judgements, failing the descriptor.

width.minimum: Given a design context, select and justify at least two technology choices (e.g. material + tool, or process + component) with reference to the design requirements.
width.typical: Justify selection decisions across materials, tools, equipment, processes and components for a design project — referencing requirements such as sustainability, safety, accessibility, cost, weight and performance; explain why alternatives were not selected and what the implications of different choices would be.
wider: Justify the selection of low-emission paints and locally sourced materials (e.g. bamboo CLT) for a specific building application — evaluate the sustainability, structural and cost implications
Justify technology selection for minimising product weight to reduce transport costs in a rural Australian context — analyse what properties must be balanced and what the selection criteria are
Evaluate a design decision to use compressive vs tensile materials in a structural application — calculate or estimate the relevant forces and justify the selection

modes.reason: Justification requires students to reason from requirement to selection to trade-off — without this structure, students select by familiarity or preference rather than by analysed fit. The scaffold (what does this application require? → which options meet each requirement? → what are the trade-offs? → which combination best fits?) produces genuine justification.

descriptors.title: Analyse needs, develop design brief, select materials
descriptors.description: analyse needs or opportunities for designing; develop design briefs; and investigate, analyse and select materials, systems, components, tools and equipment to create designed solutions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can analyse needs or opportunities for designing, and investigate and select materials, systems, components, tools and equipment (AC9TDE8P01). They can develop basic design briefs. They have not yet developed design briefs independently that incorporate universal design or Safety by Design principles, nor analysed intellectual property rights in design contexts, nor interviewed community members to identify design needs.
descriptors.endpoint: Students independently analyse needs or opportunities for designing; develop design briefs that incorporate user needs and ethical considerations; and investigate, analyse and select materials, systems, components, tools and equipment for designed solutions.
elaborations: analysing First Nations Australians' traditional grains for their potential for providing nutritional and commercial solutions
analysing the design of new products to identify how well design ideas respond to sustainability issues
developing design briefs that take into consideration the needs of users, for example universal design principles or Safety by Design principles
analysing a range of design and technologies ideas including those that draw on the intellectual property of others, including Indigenous cultural and intellectual property rights
considering the needs of community groups to identify rich design tasks, for example interviewing community members about accessibility requirements
examining tools, techniques, equipment and relationships of properties for complementary materials

nodes.label: Analysing needs and design opportunities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse a need or opportunity for designing, including considering the needs of diverse users and communities.
criteria: Identifies a specific need grounded in user or context analysis — not just a product category
Describes at least two distinct user needs that the designed solution must address
nodes.hinge_reason: Shallow needs analysis produces a design brief at N2 that does not capture real user and sustainability requirements — a brief built on assumed needs drives design criteria and material selection at N3 that cannot be validated against actual stakeholder needs.

width.minimum: Identify a genuine need or design opportunity from a given scenario; describe at least two user needs that a designed solution should address.
width.typical: Analyse a need or opportunity by investigating users, context and constraints; identify how different users (including diverse or community groups) have different needs; consider how sustainability, accessibility and Safety by Design principles shape what the designed solution must achieve.
wider: Analyse First Nations Australians' traditional grains (e.g. acacia) for their commercial and nutritional potential — develop a design opportunity statement that responds to this as a design brief starting point
Interview community members about accessibility requirements to identify an unmet need — document what the interviews revealed that desk research would not have found
Analyse new products designed to address sustainability issues (e.g. pool sanitisation, UV disinfection, disposable alternatives) — evaluate how well each responds to the identified need

modes.reason: Need analysis looks different for different user groups and contexts — a community accessibility need is identified differently from a sustainability opportunity or a commercial product gap. Multiple contexts build analytical flexibility in need identification.

nodes.label: Developing a design brief
nodes.checkpoint: Students can independently develop a design brief that defines the problem, identifies user needs, and establishes the scope and constraints of a designed solution.
criteria: Brief names a specific problem (not just a domain or product type)
At least two user needs are stated and connected to the problem
At least one constraint or scope boundary is explicit
nodes.hinge_reason: A design brief without specific constraints and assessable criteria makes N3 material and technology selection arbitrary — students cannot justify selections against criteria that don't exist, and the entire design rationale collapses.

width.minimum: Write a design brief that names the problem, identifies at least two user needs, and states at least one constraint or scope boundary.
width.typical: Develop a design brief independently that incorporates: a clear problem definition, identified user needs (including diverse users), sustainability and ethical considerations, universal design or Safety by Design principles where relevant, and scope and constraints that define what the solution will and will not address.
wider: Develop a design brief for a community need by iterating through consultation with community members — document how the brief changed through consultation
Develop a design brief that explicitly addresses Indigenous cultural and intellectual property rights — explain what considerations this adds to the brief that a standard brief would not include
Compare a brief developed from desk research alone with one developed through user interviews — analyse what the interviews added and why it matters

modes.reason: A design brief is a reasoning document — students who write briefs by filling in a template without connecting user needs to constraints to scope produce briefs that don't actually define the problem. The reasoning chain (who is this for? → what do they need? → what constrains the solution? → what is in/out of scope?) is what makes a brief useful.

nodes.label: Investigating, analysing and selecting materials, systems, components, tools and equipment
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate, analyse and select appropriate materials, systems, components, tools and equipment for a design project with justification.
criteria: At least two options are investigated for a key material or component
Selection is justified with reference to at least one criterion from the design brief

width.minimum: Investigate at least two options for a key material, component or tool; analyse each against at least one criterion from the design brief; select one and justify the choice.
width.typical: Investigate a range of materials, systems, components, tools and equipment relevant to the design project; analyse each against criteria from the design brief (including sustainability, safety, cost, performance); select and justify choices; examine the compressive and tensile properties of structural materials where relevant.
wider: Investigate materials that raise intellectual property considerations — including Indigenous cultural and intellectual property rights — and explain how these must be addressed in the design process
Research a specialist material (e.g. bioplastic, composite) and evaluate whether it is appropriate for the design project given its properties, availability, cost and sustainability
Justify selections that prioritise sustainability over conventional choices — explain what you would accept as a trade-off and what you would not

descriptors.title: Generate, test, iterate and communicate design ideas
descriptors.description: apply innovation and enterprise skills to generate, test, iterate and communicate design ideas, processes and solutions, including using digital tools
descriptors.knowledge: Students can generate, test, iterate and communicate design ideas, processes and solutions (AC9TDE8P02). They have experience with ideation techniques, modelling and design documentation. They have not yet applied innovation and enterprise skills, reimagined designs to feature emerging technologies, or used the full range of technical drawing and 3D modelling/prototyping tools at this level.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply innovation and enterprise skills to generate, test, iterate and communicate design ideas and solutions — using analysis of benefits and constraints, a range of modelling and prototyping techniques, and appropriate technical documentation for an intended audience.
elaborations: using techniques including combining and modifying ideas and exploring functionality to generate solution concepts and reimagining designs to feature emerging technologies
undertaking functional, structural and aesthetic analysis of benefits and constraints of design ideas, for example assessing how a design is suitable for different communities and environments
considering competing variables that may hinder or enhance project development
producing drawings, models and prototypes to explore design ideas, for example using technical drawing techniques, 3D printers or augmented reality modelling software
communicating using appropriate technical terms and recording the generation and development of design ideas and processes
using design thinking and enterprise skills to create innovative approaches to processes and solutions

nodes.label: Generating ideas with innovation and enterprise thinking
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use innovation and enterprise thinking to generate design concepts, including reimagining existing designs and incorporating emerging technologies.
criteria: At least two distinct design concepts are generated — not variations of the same approach
At least one concept reflects innovation or enterprise thinking beyond conventional solutions

width.minimum: Generate at least two distinct design concepts using at least one innovation or enterprise technique; concepts should be different approaches, not variants of the same solution.
width.typical: Apply innovation and enterprise skills — brainstorming novel ideas inspired by nature, transforming a solution for a target market, reimagining designs with emerging technologies — to generate a range of design concepts; consider competing variables (weight, strength, price, sustainability, user needs, community consultation) that may shape or constrain the concepts.
wider: Use nature-inspired design (biomimicry) as an ideation framework — generate concepts that translate a natural mechanism or structure into a designed solution
Generate concepts that respond to an identified enterprise opportunity — explain what market gap or user need each concept addresses and how it would be communicated to a target market
Design wearable technology concepts that incorporate emerging technologies (e.g. biometric sensing) to provide independence for elderly or health-focused users

nodes.label: Functional, structural and aesthetic analysis
nodes.checkpoint: Students can undertake functional, structural and aesthetic analysis of design ideas, identifying benefits and constraints for different communities and environments.
criteria: Analysis addresses at least two of the three dimensions explicitly
Identifies a genuine benefit and a genuine constraint — not just positive descriptions
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who analyse design ideas on only one dimension produce prototypes at N3 that test one factor and ignore the others — the prototype does not represent the full design intent and N4 communication cannot justify multi-factor decisions that were never made.

width.minimum: Analyse one design idea against at least two of the three dimensions (functional, structural, aesthetic); identify one benefit and one constraint.
width.typical: Undertake functional, structural and aesthetic analysis of multiple design ideas; identify benefits and constraints for different communities and environments; consider how the same design might need to be adapted for a different context (e.g. for use in a different region or for accessibility requirements).
wider: Analyse a design for suitability in a challenging environment — for example, how skyscraper design adapts structurally and functionally for earthquake zones such as Japan

Analyse a design for accessibility across different user populations — identify what functional or structural changes would be required for the design to serve users with different physical requirements
Compare the same design brief resolved for two different cultural or geographic contexts — analyse how different constraints produce different design solutions

modes.reason: Three-dimension analysis (functional, structural, aesthetic) requires a systematic framework — students who analyse without structure tend to describe the design rather than evaluate it against these specific lenses. A scaffold (what does it do? → how does it hold up? → how does it look and feel to use?) produces genuine analysis.

nodes.label: Producing drawings, models and prototypes
