nodes.checkpoint: Students can produce drawings, models and prototypes using appropriate techniques and digital tools to explore and develop design ideas.
criteria: Produces at least one representation with sufficient detail that another person could understand the design
Can explain what aspect of the design the representation communicates

width.minimum: Produce at least one visual or physical representation of a design idea using a drawing technique or modelling tool; explain what aspect of the design the representation communicates.
width.typical: Produce multiple representations of design ideas using a range of techniques — technical drawings (perspective, orthogonal), digital imaging, 3D modelling or 3D printing, or AR modelling; use prototypes to explore aesthetic considerations and test functional ideas; explain what each representation communicates that the others don't.
wider: Produce multiple prototypes that show an understanding of competing aesthetic considerations — explain how each prototype prioritises different aesthetic factors and what user feedback would help choose between them
Use 3D printing or AR modelling software to prototype a design — explain what this representation reveals that 2D drawing cannot
Produce a technical drawing (orthogonal and perspective) of the same design and explain how each representation serves a different stage or audience in the design process

modes.reason: Prototype fidelity develops through accumulation — students who have only produced sketches cannot judge what a physical prototype tests that a sketch doesn't. Multiple representation types build the ability to match representation type to design purpose.

nodes.label: Communicating design ideas and processes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can communicate design ideas, processes and solutions using appropriate technical language and documentation for an intended audience.
criteria: Documentation uses appropriate technical language
At least one design decision is justified — not just described

width.minimum: Document at least one stage of a design process with sufficient detail and appropriate technical language for the intended audience to follow.
width.typical: Develop documentation (e.g. a digital portfolio) that communicates each step of the design process using appropriate technical terms, images and text; justify design decisions made at key stages; ensure communication is tailored to the intended audience.
wider: Produce a digital portfolio with images and text that clearly communicates each step of a design process — explain how the documentation decisions were made for the intended audience
Justify design decisions in the documentation including trade-offs made, alternatives considered, and sustainability rationale
Develop a design communication package for an enterprise context — pitching the design concept to a target market audience rather than a technical audience

descriptors.title: Select, justify, test and make designed solutions
descriptors.description: select, justify, test and use suitable technologies, skills and processes, and apply safety procedures to safely make designed solutions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can select, justify and use suitable materials, components, tools, equipment and techniques safely (AC9TDE8P03). They have experience with safe production practices. They have not yet worked with full production independence, adapted processes to unforeseen challenges, or experimented with innovative material combinations at this level.
descriptors.endpoint: Students select, justify, test and use suitable technologies, skills and processes with independence and appropriate safety procedures to safely make designed solutions — including adapting processes to risks and unforeseen challenges.
elaborations: refining technical skills and using production skills with independence to produce quality designed solutions
using materials, components, tools, equipment and techniques safely and considering alternatives to maximise sustainability
experimenting with innovative combinations and ways of manipulating traditional and contemporary materials and recording findings in a collaborative space
modifying production processes to respond to opportunities, risks or unforeseen challenges
experimenting with the functional and sensory properties of food to determine the most successful approach

nodes.label: Independent and safe production practice
nodes.checkpoint: Students can set up and use tools, equipment and techniques independently and safely, applying appropriate personal protective equipment and safe working practices for the specific design project.
criteria: Sets up and operates at least one tool or piece of equipment independently
Applies appropriate safe working practices without being prompted
nodes.hinge_reason: Independent safe production is prerequisite for N2 — students who cannot operate tools and equipment safely and independently cannot conduct the experimental material combinations that N2 requires without constant supervision, which prevents genuine experimentation.

width.minimum: Independently set up and use at least one tool or piece of equipment relevant to the design project; demonstrate appropriate safe working practices without supervision prompts.
width.typical: Demonstrate independent safe working practice across the production process — including selecting and setting up equipment appropriately, wearing appropriate PPE, identifying hazards in the production process, and applying risk-reduction strategies without prompting.
wider: Independently set up a specific machine (e.g. lathe) to produce a part to specified dimensions — explain each setup step and the safety rationale for each
Review production safety for a group project and identify risks for each team member's role — develop safety protocols for the shared production environment

modes.reason: Safe production practice is procedural and requires sufficient hands-on repetition to become genuinely independent. Students who have only observed or worked with close supervision are not yet operating independently. Practice in context-specific setups (the actual tools and materials of the project) is the path to independence.

nodes.label: Experimenting with material combinations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can experiment with combinations and manipulation of traditional and contemporary materials, components, tools and techniques, and evaluate their findings.
criteria: Experiments with at least two material or technique approaches
Records findings in enough detail that the experiment could be replicated
Evaluates which approach better meets the design requirements and why

width.minimum: Experiment with at least two ways of using or combining a material or technique; record findings and explain which approach was more effective and why.
width.typical: Experiment with innovative combinations of materials, components and techniques — including contemporary and traditional materials; record findings collaboratively; debate the merits of different approaches with peers; consider sustainability in material choice (e.g. materials that store carbon or reduce demand for less sustainable alternatives).
wider: Experiment with food prepared three different ways to maximise colour, flavour and nutritive value — evaluate which approach best meets the design criteria for a specific food solution
Investigate how a traditional material (e.g. timber) performs compared to a manufactured alternative for a specific application — test for relevant properties and make a justified selection
Experiment with a combination of materials not previously used together — document findings in a shared space and evaluate the combination against the design requirements

modes.reason: Material combination judgements develop through accumulated experimental experience — a single combination test does not provide the comparative base needed to evaluate merits. Multiple experiments across different material types build the experiential repertoire that meaningful evaluation requires.

nodes.label: Adapting production to risks and challenges
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and respond to risks, unexpected challenges and opportunities that arise during production, modifying processes to maintain quality and sustainability.
criteria: Identifies at least one specific production risk or challenge
Describes a specific adaptation made or proposed — not just a general safety principle

width.minimum: Identify at least one risk or unexpected challenge that arose or could arise during production; describe how you responded or would respond to maintain quality or safety.
width.typical: Monitor production for risks and unexpected challenges (material faults, workload coordination issues, changed conditions); respond by modifying production processes appropriately; maintain a record of adaptations made and explain the reasoning behind each; maximise sustainability in choices made under constraint.
wider: Document and reflect on a production adaptation made in response to an unforeseen challenge (e.g. material fault, unexpected cooking result) — evaluate whether the adaptation maintained quality and what you would do differently
Plan contingencies for identified production risks before production begins — implement contingency procedures when a risk materialises and evaluate their effectiveness
Analyse how bulk food production introduces coordination and scaling challenges — experiment with adapting a recipe for bulk production and evaluate the impact on quality and safety

descriptors.title: Develop design criteria and evaluate independently
descriptors.description: develop design criteria independently including sustainability to evaluate design ideas, processes and solutions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can develop design criteria collaboratively including sustainability to evaluate design ideas, processes and solutions (AC9TDE8P04). They have experience using criteria to guide evaluation. They have not yet developed criteria independently, reflected substantively on process choices, or iterated based on evaluation feedback.
descriptors.endpoint: Students independently develop design criteria including sustainability and use them to evaluate and iterate design ideas, processes and solutions — including reflecting on process choices and responding creatively to evaluation feedback.
elaborations: establishing specific design criteria for evaluating designed solutions, for example determining necessary function of a product and making a judgement about whether these have been met after stress testing or user testing
evaluating and justifying the use and best combination of traditional, contemporary and emerging technologies during project development, including consideration of sustainability
reflecting on learning including processes or choices made at various stages of a design process and modifying plans when needed with consideration of design criteria
responding creatively to evaluation feedback to iterate and modify design ideas and processes to improve sustainability measures

nodes.label: Independently developing design criteria
nodes.checkpoint: Students can independently develop specific, assessable design criteria that include sustainability considerations.
criteria: At least two criteria are specific and assessable — a person could check whether a solution meets them
At least one sustainability criterion is included
nodes.hinge_reason: The descriptor specifies criteria developed independently — if students cannot do this at N1, N2 evaluation and N3 reflection are conducted against criteria that are not their own, and the descriptor's core demand is not met.

width.minimum: Write at least two design criteria independently (without a provided template); criteria must be assessable against a designed solution and include at least one sustainability criterion.
width.typical: Develop a set of design criteria independently from the design brief — including functional, aesthetic, safety, sustainability and user experience criteria; ensure each criterion is specific and assessable; explain the reasoning behind key criteria choices.
wider: Develop criteria that explicitly specify acceptable performance thresholds (e.g. maximum load for a structure, acceptable stress test result) — not just what is required but how it will be measured
Develop criteria that address the full product life cycle, not just the use phase — including criteria for material sourcing, production impact and end-of-life
Compare criteria developed independently with criteria developed through user consultation — analyse what consultation adds

modes.reason: Independent criteria development requires students to reason from the design brief to testable statements. Students who develop criteria without this process produce vague or circular criteria (e.g. 'the product should look good'). The reasoning path (what must this solution do? → how would we know if it did? → what sustainability considerations apply?) produces actionable criteria.

nodes.label: Evaluating and justifying technology use against criteria
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate and justify the use of traditional, contemporary and emerging technologies during a design project against design criteria including sustainability.
criteria: Evaluation references specific design criteria — not general preferences
Justification explains why the chosen technology meets the criteria better than an alternative
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot evaluate technology choices against criteria at N2 cannot identify what to reflect on and iterate at N3 — reflection without prior evaluation produces generalised commentary rather than specific design improvements.

width.minimum: Evaluate at least one technology choice made during the project against at least one design criterion; explain whether the choice met the criterion and why.
width.typical: Evaluate and justify technology use across the project — including justification for choosing traditional, contemporary or emerging technologies; apply sustainability criteria to technology choices; evaluate decisions at multiple stages of the project, not just the final solution.
wider: Evaluate and justify farming method choices (e.g. from South-East Asia) against sustainability criteria — explain what the evaluation revealed about the relationship between traditional practice and contemporary sustainability requirements
Compare the sustainability implications of two competing technologies for the same task in the project — make a justified selection and explain what you would trade off
Evaluate whether a technology choice that is superior on performance criteria is inferior on sustainability criteria — make and justify a final decision

modes.reason: Technology evaluation against criteria requires students to reason systematically — for each technology choice, does it meet this criterion? why? what trade-off is made? Students who evaluate by intuition produce justifications that cannot ground the specific iterations required at N3.

nodes.label: Reflecting on process and iterating
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on process choices made at various stages of a design process and iterate design ideas to improve outcomes, including sustainability.
criteria: Reflection identifies a specific process choice — not just a general description of what was done
Reflection includes a judgement about effectiveness and what would be done differently

width.minimum: Reflect on at least one process choice made during the project — explain what was decided, whether it was effective, and what you would do differently.
width.typical: Reflect on learning across the design process — identify choices made at multiple stages that shaped the outcome; evaluate the effectiveness of each; modify plans when needed with reference to design criteria; respond to evaluation feedback by iterating design ideas to improve sustainability or other criteria.
wider: Document and reflect on a full iteration cycle — what feedback prompted the iteration, what was changed, and whether the change improved the solution against the criteria
Reflect on a process choice that prioritised one criterion at the cost of another — evaluate whether the trade-off was justified in hindsight
Use evaluation feedback to explore sustainable material substitutions (e.g. plant-based timber oils, bioplastics) — document the iteration and evaluate the improvement

descriptors.title: Develop project plans for time, cost, risk and production
descriptors.description: develop project plans for intended purposes and audiences to individually and collaboratively manage projects, taking into consideration time, cost, risk, processes and production of designed solutions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can develop project plans to individually and collaboratively manage time, cost and production (AC9TDE8P05). They have experience with sequencing and tracking tasks. They have not yet developed plans for specific intended purposes and audiences, incorporated formal risk and contingency planning, or investigated manufacturing process strategies for production enhancement.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop project plans for intended purposes and audiences that manage time, cost, risk, processes and production of designed solutions — including flowcharts, spreadsheets, equitable role distribution, contingencies, and production enhancement strategies.
elaborations: producing, explaining and interpreting drawings and planning production timelines using digital tools, for example establishing materials and equipment needs using spreadsheets, or creating production flowcharts
collaborating to develop production plans for equitable distribution of work including discussing roles, tasks and deadlines and considering flexibility and contingencies
investigating manufacturing processes to identify strategies to enhance production, for example identifying techniques to reduce use, cut costs, speed up processes or to form beneficial partnerships

nodes.label: Planning and interpreting production timelines
nodes.checkpoint: Students can produce, explain and interpret drawings and production timelines using digital tools for a design project.
criteria: Production plan is produced using a digital tool with at least three sequenced tasks
At least one task dependency is identified and explained
nodes.hinge_reason: A production plan that cannot be interpreted by collaborators makes N2 equitable role distribution impossible — if the timeline and task structure are unclear, team members cannot negotiate distribution or identify their responsibilities.

width.minimum: Produce a production timeline using a digital tool; include at least three tasks with timeframes and dependencies; explain one dependency between tasks.
width.typical: Produce and interpret production timelines and flowcharts using digital tools (spreadsheets, planning software); include task dependencies, resource requirements and sequencing logic; explain how the timeline supports efficient, safe and sustainable workflows.
wider: Create a production flowchart that maps all decision points in a production process — explain how the flowchart identifies where safety checks, quality reviews or sustainability decisions occur
Produce a materials and equipment needs analysis using a spreadsheet — calculate quantities, costs and sourcing requirements for the production plan
Compare two approaches to sequencing the same production tasks — explain which produces a more efficient workflow and why

modes.reason: Production timeline creation requires precision — task sequence, dependencies, durations and milestones must be specific enough to be actionable. Students who produce vague plans cannot use them for collaboration or risk identification.

nodes.label: Collaborative planning with equitable role distribution
nodes.checkpoint: Students can collaboratively develop a production plan with equitable distribution of roles, tasks and deadlines, including flexibility and contingencies.
criteria: All team members have assigned roles and tasks in the plan
At least one contingency is documented for an identified risk

width.minimum: In a collaborative project, assign roles and tasks to all team members with deadlines; identify at least one contingency if a task is delayed or a person is unavailable.
width.typical: Collaboratively develop a production plan that distributes work equitably — assign roles and tasks based on skills and availability; discuss and agree on deadlines and flexibility; build contingencies for foreseeable risks; monitor and adjust the plan as the project progresses.
wider: Reflect on the equity of role distribution in a completed collaborative project — evaluate whether the plan achieved equitable contribution and what changes would improve future plans
Develop a contingency plan that addresses at least three distinct risks (material, personnel, timeline) — test the contingency plan by simulating a specific risk event
Investigate how professional design and manufacturing teams structure equitable collaboration — identify what practices could be applied to student projects

nodes.label: Strategies to enhance production
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate manufacturing processes to identify strategies that enhance production — reducing waste, cutting costs, speeding up processes or forming beneficial production partnerships.
criteria: Identifies at least one production enhancement strategy that is specific to the design project
Explains what it improves and how it would be implemented — not just names the strategy

width.minimum: Identify at least one strategy to enhance a production process; explain what it reduces or improves and why.
width.typical: Investigate manufacturing processes to identify multiple production enhancement strategies — waste reduction, cost reduction, speed improvement, process optimisation or beneficial partnerships; evaluate each strategy for its practical applicability to the design project; incorporate selected strategies into the project plan.
wider: Investigate lean manufacturing or similar production improvement frameworks — identify which principles apply to the design project and explain how they would change the production plan
Identify where in the production process beneficial partnerships (e.g. with specialist manufacturers, suppliers or fabricators) could reduce cost, time or complexity — evaluate the trade-offs
Map production waste at each stage of a design project and identify reduction strategies — evaluate the sustainability benefit of each strategy

modes.reason: Production enhancement requires students to reason from current process → identify inefficiency or waste → identify strategy → evaluate applicability. Without this structure, students suggest generic improvements without analysing whether they apply to their specific production context.
